statement: A use case does not need to be 'best' to be valuable; even a mediocre but readable use case is useful, and is often more useful than the competing requirements documents teams produce, so writers should aim for readable rather than perfect.
Writing use cases is fundamentally an exercise in natural-language essay/prose writing, which is why articulating what makes a use case 'good' (and how to produce one) is inherently difficult.

The value and life of a use case is in its text, not its graphics; UML use-case diagram notation neither adds to nor constrains the textual content, so writing effort belongs on the prose rather than the diagram.

There is no single best use-case template or writing process; template, format, and precision recommendations should vary with each project's needs, group values, priorities, and system characteristics.
condition: different projects have different needs, values, priorities, and system characteristics

statement: Software development is fundamentally a cooperative game of group invention and communication, and the primary purpose of a use case is to communicate with its readers, so use-case writing should be optimized for reader understanding.

Write use cases with two complementary work orders: top-down (system scope, then actors, then goals, then the main success story, then alternative conditions and paths) and middle-out (start at the user-goal level, work up to strategic goals, then down to subfunctions).
Get clear about the design scope of the system being described before writing its use cases.

Brainstorm all the actors — human and non-human — that have an operational goal against the system, and brainstorm all of their goals against the system over its entire lifetime, double-checking for time-based and other events that make the system react.
Write the actor-goal list, then double-check, prioritize, merge, and reconsider the goals on it.
Actors are only there to help you find all the use cases; the goals, not the actors, are the point.

Work the scope outward by defining the system that contains the system under discussion, extend each goal outward to find who really cares about achieving it, and add the resulting primary-actor goals to the list of use cases to write.
For each use case, brainstorm the stakeholders, write how their interests are satisfied at successful conclusion, and write which interests must be protected if the use case fails.
Write the precondition as what the system has already ensured is certainly true, and write the event or trigger that starts the main success scenario.
Write each main-success-scenario step as a goal succeeding that distinctly moves the process forward, showing the intent of the actor — what they want and get accomplished in that step.
Avoid user-interface descriptions in use-case action steps.
Manage the level of goal accomplishment so that the main success scenario is between 3 and 11 steps long.
condition: applies to the main success scenario

statement: After drafting, verify that the interests of all stakeholders are fully met and that the sequencing requirements among steps (or the lack of such requirements) are clear.
Brainstorm the failures and alternative paths, but include only the failures the system itself must detect and handle.

Write each failure or alternative as a condition phrase plus a scenario fragment showing how that course leads to goal failure or an alternative success, using the same writing rules as the main success scenario.
Update the main success scenario with any new validations discovered while writing the extensions.
Move any sub-goal that grows too complex to fit neatly into the current use case out into its own sub use case.

A use case is a description of the possible sequences of interactions (scenarios) between the system under discussion and its external actors in pursuit of a particular goal, collecting both the scenarios where the goal is achieved and those where it must be abandoned.
Use cases describe the system's externally visible responsibilities and behavior — how it responds to the outside world — without revealing how its internal parts are constructed.

Use cases are fundamentally a text-based documentation form whose main purpose is to communicate from one person to another, often to readers with no special informatics training, so simple text is usually the best choice over diagrams.
Each use case is associated with the goal of one particular actor, the primary actor, and collects all the scenarios related to that primary actor's goal.

A system-in-use story (user story) is a single, highly specific concrete example of one named actor using the system; use it to warm up and to anchor the use case, but it is not itself the requirements.

Keep a system-in-use story brief enough to grasp at a glance, yet include the actor's details, motives, and emotional content so every downstream reader can see how the system should add value to the user.

Use cases form only the behavioral/functional portion of the requirements file (roughly one chapter), not the entire requirements; business rules, glossary, performance targets, and process requirements belong in their own sections.

Use-case names act as the hub of a wheel for the requirements file: they provide a framework on which to hang other project details (priority, teaming, release dates, status, performance, interface channels) and link otherwise-disconnected information.
'Dressed' use cases use a sentence-numbering scheme and named template fields, whereas 'casual' use cases short-circuit some of the numbering and fields; the appropriate dress varies by situation.
condition: the degree of formality depends on the project situation

statement: Manage your writing energy by capturing an outline and the essence of each use case first and adding details later, rather than writing all details in one sitting; this lets stakeholders correct priorities early and lets the work be split across groups for parallelism.

Precision (how much detail you choose to state) is not the same as accuracy (correctness): a low-precision statement of goals can communicate a great deal and still be accurate, while a high-precision statement can be precisely wrong.
Get the goal list accurate at low precision before expending the energy of a fully elaborated, high-precision use-case set, because high-precision detail built on an inaccurate goal is wasted energy.

Write use cases in four staged passes that match increasing precision, reviewing and pausing after each: (1) list actors and their goals, (2) write the stakeholders, trigger, and main success scenario, (3) brainstorm the failure conditions, (4) write the failure handling.

Draft the complete list of failure/extension conditions before working out how the system handles any of them, because writers who start writing failure handling immediately tend to run out of energy before they have listed all the failure conditions.
Writing failure handling is often tricky and surprising work because it frequently surfaces an obscure business rule or reveals a new actor or goal that must be supported.
Not all use cases on a project need to be written exactly the same way; how much variation in style a project can tolerate (its tolerance) is itself a project decision.

A high-ceremony (high-density, hardened) practice relies on uniform work-products and formalized activities and tolerates little variation, whereas a low-ceremony (casual) practice relies on person-to-person communication to cover missing information and writer-to-writer variation.

Match use-case formality to project risk: large or life-critical projects warrant a hardened, fully dressed, low-tolerance template with high-ceremony reviews, while small low-damage projects warrant a casual, low-density template with optional fields and higher tolerance.
condition: the appropriate template density, tolerance, and ceremony depend on the project's criticality, size, and priorities

statement: There is no single correct use-case template; provide at least two — a casual template for low-ceremony projects and a fully dressed template adaptable to higher-ceremony projects.

Choosing template, tolerance, and ceremony must be done project by project: stating only that 'use cases will be used' is an incomplete process definition, because you must also specify when fully dressed versus casual use cases apply, which template parts are mandatory, and how much tolerance is permitted.
How you evaluate the quality of your use cases depends on the tolerance, density, and ceremony adopted on the project, so no fixed set of quality measures applies across all projects.
Characterize a project for choosing ceremony by three factors: the number of people being coordinated, the potential for damage, and the key development priorities.
On a project coordinating many writers, standardize carefully on one template (casual or dressed) because writer variation will already be large and inconsistency confuses readers and costs rework.
condition: many writers are involved

statement: An actor is anything that has behavior — a person, organization, computer system, or hardware/software — and is more precisely a role (a category of person such as a job description or relationship).

Normally write a use case with the system under discussion as an unopened black box, not mentioning internal actors, and open it into a white-box use case only when you need to describe how the system's internal pieces work together to deliver externally visible behavior.
exception: open the black box as a white-box use case to show how internal actors deliver externally visible behavior, common for business use cases

statement: The primary actor of a use case is the one external actor whose goal the use case satisfies and whose action initiates it; prefer to name the stakeholder whose goal it is rather than the technological operator, so you know to whom the use case brings value.
A secondary actor is an external actor that provides a service to the system under discussion; collect the secondary actors to identify the external interfaces and protocols the system will use.

'Secondary' does not mean unimportant and 'primary' does not mean most important; do not relabel a secondary actor as primary to avoid forgetting it, because it will already be captured as a secondary actor with its interface.
For a use case triggered by time (such as midnight or month-end) with no initiating operator, name as the primary actor whoever cares that the use case runs, in order to know to whom it brings value.
condition: the use case is triggered by time rather than by an operator

statement: Brainstorm the actors first as a structured way to brainstorm all the goals; it is really goal coverage you are after, so several actors sharing one goal does no harm and a missed hard-to-find goal will be caught by other parts of the exercise.

Primary actors matter most at two points — early requirements gathering and just before delivery — and are relatively unimportant in between, so do not fuss over the exact primary-actor name during detailed writing, since a use case can serve multiple actor types and names become generic.

Err toward over-listing actors early, because the cost of missing an actor (omitting an entire section of requirements, discovered late) is far higher than the cost of having too many actors (a little extra early work to eliminate the unnecessary ones).

Just before delivery the primary-actor list is needed again — to partition the system into delivery packages per user machine, to set per-use-case security levels, and to build training curricula by user classification.

A stakeholder is anyone with a vested interest in the use case's behavior even if they never interact with the system (for example owners or regulatory bodies); every primary actor is a stakeholder, but many stakeholders have no use cases of their own.

Stakeholders do not appear directly in the text of a use case; their interests are captured in the system's behavior — the checks and validations it performs, the logs it creates, and the actions it takes.

A use case is a form of contract that reconciles the possibly conflicting interests of all stakeholders, so the specified system behavior must protect the interests of stakeholders who are not present to defend their own interests.

Produce an Actor List as a two-column table — the actor name/role and a characterization of that actor type's skills and goals — to keep the end users' characteristics in front of the team during development; it is relatively valuable but not crucial.

Distinguish functional scope (which functions you choose to deliver, managed with a goal list marking each goal in scope / out of scope / next release) from design scope (the extent of the system you are charged with building).
Resolve scope ambiguity with an in/out list — a three-column table of topic, in, out — adding any topic whose scope might be unclear and asking the group to mark it in or out.
Design scope is the boundary of the system: the set of hardware and software you are charged with designing; everything you only interface with lies outside that scope.
Getting design scope wrong is expensive — for example, mistaking whether a component is in scope can throw a fixed-price bid off by a factor of two or more and lead to building the wrong system.
Label every use case with its design scope, because the in/out boundary is obvious to a single writer but invisible to multiple readers and writers, who otherwise misread the requirements.

Give explicit names to your design scopes and broadcast the definitions; useful scope levels are corporate/organization (the whole company), system (the named piece you build), and subsystem (an opened-up part of that system).
Business use cases are typically written at corporate or departmental scope.

Write at least one wide, corporate-scope use case by finding the outermost primary actor for the system and showing how the system satisfies that actor's goal; these few high-level use cases tie together many lower-level system-scope use cases.

The basic Actors and Goals model is that actors have goals against other actors: the primary actor's goal calls upon the system's declared responsibility, so a responsibility and a goal are often the same phrase stated two ways.

Goals can fail — from bad primary-actor data, an internal failure, or a secondary actor failing its promised service — so stating how the system behaves on intermediate goal failure (goal repair) and on outright goal failure is a critical part of the functional requirements.

The primary actor stays responsible for its overall goal even when the system fails and so needs a backup plan; capturing goal failures and the system's failure responses is a major reason use cases make excellent functional requirements.

An interaction may be a single message or a whole sequence of interactions, and a sequence can be folded up into one higher-level phrase or unfolded into smaller steps, which is why the set of use cases behaves as an ever-unfolding story.

Because future interactions are not fully determined like the past, describe them as a set of possible sequences — one sequence per condition of the world — each characterized by the conditions under which it occurs and its outcome (goal success or goal failure); that set is the use case and each sequence is a scenario.

The single hardest part of writing effective use cases is choosing the right level of detail for the reader, staying consistent at that level, and making sure the reader knows which level you are writing at.

Use-case step order is strictly a partial ordering rather than a fixed sequence; handle steps that may occur in any order with plain natural language (for example 'in any order') instead of inventing a formal ordering notation.

A scenario is a sequence of interactions occurring under certain conditions with the intent of achieving the primary actor's goal; it starts at the triggering action and continues until the goal is delivered or abandoned and the system has completed its responsibilities for that interaction.

Even though the basic definition omits it, the use case must capture what the system actually does internally — its checks and validations (such as security clearance or sufficient balance) and standing responsibilities such as logging every interaction or releasing resources — or the scenario would end with those responsibilities unmet.

Every action a system performs exists to satisfy or protect some stakeholder's interest (for example, logging interactions for auditors, or checking the balance for the bank owner), so a use case is fundamentally an agreement among the stakeholders about how the system behaves.

Under the Stakeholders and Interests model, list the stakeholders and their interests in the use case and use that list to check that every interest is protected; every system action should further or protect a stakeholder interest, and ideally every interest is delivered at successful completion.

Every scenario step is an action of exactly one of three kinds: an interaction between two actors, a validation, or an internal state change; validations and state changes exist to protect a stakeholder's interest.

A success scenario ends with all agreed-upon stakeholder interests satisfied, a failure scenario ends with all agreed-upon interests protected despite the failure, and scenario writing ends only when every stakeholder interest is either satisfied or protected.
A use case may be triggered by the primary actor initiating an interaction with the system, by the primary actor acting through an intermediary, or by a time- or state-based event.

Adopting the Stakeholders and Interests model changes the writing procedure only slightly: briefly list the stakeholders and their interests and use the list as a double-check that none was inadvertently omitted; the rest of the writing is unchanged.

Goals unfold into smaller goals across an unbounded range, but three levels suffice for use-case work: user-goal ('blue', 'sea level'), strategic ('white', above blue), and subfunction ('indigo', below blue, with 'black' marking a goal too low to expand).

The user-goal ('blue') level is the goal of a primary actor getting one unit of work done in a single sitting; test it by asking whether it is done by one person in one place at one time (about 2–20 minutes), whether you could go to lunch once it is complete, and whether doing many of them would justify a raise — by which 'log on' fails but 'register a new customer' passes.

Justify the existence of the system by the list of blue (user-goal) use cases it supports: that list is the shortest summary of the system's function and the basis for prioritization, delivery, team division, estimation, and development.

Most use cases below sea level (indigo/black subfunctions) should not be written or read on their own; one 100-page all-indigo requirements document failed its readers until it was replaced by six user-goal use cases that everyone found easier to understand.

Strategic ('white') use cases involve multiple user-goal goals and serve three purposes: showing the context the system's services must function in, showing the life-cycle sequencing of related goals, and providing a table of contents/index for the lower-level use cases.

To write a high-level (white) use case, take the system's blue goals, find the outermost design scope that still leaves the primary actor outside, gather all blue goals with that ultimate actor and scope, name the strategic goal that actor has against the system, and write a use case for it; it ties many blue use cases together and is easy for executive sponsors to review.

There are typically very few topmost-level use cases — only about five even in the largest systems — and people tend to write too many use cases at too low a level; but do not trust these white use cases as the functional requirements, which still reside in the blue use cases.

Subfunction (indigo) goals are those needed to carry out user-task goals and are included only as needed — for readability or because many higher goals share them (for example 'Find a product' or 'Save as file').
Mark a use case 'black' to signal it is too low-level to expand and that its contents should be rolled up into a higher-level use case.

Use-case levels nest by color: a white use case contains white or blue steps, a blue use case contains indigo steps, and an indigo use case contains indigo and black steps, with 'sea level' (blue) being the line where the colors change.

Spend most energy detecting and listing the blue (user-goal) use cases because those are the important ones, plan to write only a few outermost use cases for context and indexing, and do not fuss over whether a particular requirement sentence is promoted to a use-case title.

Being a use-case title does not mean 'most important' and not being one does not mean 'unimportant'; it costs nothing to break a complex scenario chunk into its own use case or fold a trivial one back, and only blue goals are guaranteed to have their own use case.

Write each goal and use-case title as an active goal phrase of the form <verb> <direct object>; whether you use the present-tense or gerund verb form does not matter, so pick one form per project and spend your energy on something more critical.

Optionally attach scope and goal-level icons to a use case — the scope logo at the top-left and the goal-level logo by the title — so a reader can see the design scope and goal level at a glance before reading.

Produce the Actor-Goal List — the blue-level use cases with their primary actors, at minimum two columns (actor; goal as a short verb phrase), optionally adding trigger, priority, or complexity — because it is the crucial negotiating point among the end-user representative, the financial sponsor, and the developers; the goals listed must be blue-level.

Put into a precondition only what the system can guarantee is true: it states something the programmers ensure has happened before the use case starts and is therefore never checked or revalidated inside the use case.

Do not put 'almost always true' conditions (things often but not necessarily true) into the precondition; record such normal-context information in the 'Context of use' section instead, and let the software handle the not-true case as one of its normal cases.
exception: conditions that are usually but not always true belong in Context of use, not the precondition

statement: Write the Success End Condition as simple assertions about the state of the world at successful completion, showing which stakeholder interests have been satisfied — usually at least the user's and the providing company's, sometimes a regulator's.
Apply this pass/fail test to a Success End Condition: every stakeholder, reading it, would agree that their interests had been satisfied for the primary actor's goal.

Use the Failed End Protection (Failure Protection) condition to capture the special interests that must be protected when the goal is abandoned, written as simple assertions about the world at abandonment (for example, 'if the ATM did not dispense cash, the account is not debited'); leave it blank when nothing interesting must be protected.

Filling out the Failure Protection condition often reveals a needed failure log or marker of how far the system got that the main success scenario never mentioned; when examining stakeholder interests surfaces such a need, add the log to the use case.
Apply this pass/fail test to a Failure Protection condition: every stakeholder would agree, reading it, that their interests are protected under failure of this goal.

Choose the main success scenario as the one typical, easy-to-understand success path that contains no failures, and build all other scenarios as extensions off it; it need not be the shortest or only success scenario, just a good base to build from.

Use cases work by exploiting the natural way people explain things — tell a simple complete story first, then add the complications ('well, actually, when such-and-such occurs...') — which is the form Jacobson found remarkably effective for describing system behavior.

The same writing style and the same three action kinds (interaction, validation, state change) are used everywhere — main scenario, extensions, business, high-level, and low-level use cases — so mastering the three action kinds equips you to write any part of any use case.

Use the core action sentence forms: 'Actor1 verbs Actor2 with some data' for an interaction, 'the system verifies that something meets some criteria' for a validation, and 'the system changes something to reflect something' for a state change.

Write every action step so it shows the process moving distinctly forward, with the amount of progress matching the goal level; a step like 'user hits the tab key' moves the process so little that you have either chosen the wrong action or are writing a too-low (deep indigo) use case.

Keep the main success scenario to roughly 11 steps or fewer; when a scenario reaches 13–17 steps the sentences usually are not moving the goal forward, and combining steps makes the text clearer and easier to read without losing essential information.
condition: applies to the main success scenario

statement: When a step does not move the process forward enough, ask 'Why is this actor doing that?'; the answer is the higher-level goal you should write instead (for example, replace 'user hits tab key' with 'user enters name and address').

Make it always clear who holds the ball: at each step exactly one actor acts (and is the subject named first or second in the sentence), doing one of three things — act on itself, pass the ball to another actor, or validate it — and you should be able to ask at each step's end who now has the ball.

Use simple 8th-grade grammar — noun, verb, direct object, prepositional phrase — and never drop the leading noun/actor, because without it the reader cannot tell who has the ball and the story becomes hard to follow.
Write from a neutral bird's-eye point of view, describing every actor with the same kinds of verbs as in a play, rather than from the system's own point of view talking to itself.

For a validation step use a goal-achieving verb such as 'verifies', 'validates', 'ensures', or 'establishes' and avoid 'checks' or 'sees whether', because 'checks' forces a non-forward-moving 'if it passed... / if it failed...' construction; let the appearance of the word 'if' trigger you to rephrase.
Each step must show the intent (the semantics) of the actor — what they want to accomplish and what information must pass — not the step-by-step user-interface dialog of their particular movements.

Keep user-interface dialog out of the requirements because it makes the document longer, harder to read, and costlier to maintain, is usually not a real requirement, is brittle to design changes, and usurps the UI designer's job; the user-task-level use cases that capture only interface semantics are Constantine and Lockwood's 'essential use cases', the most important ones for system design.
Mention the timing of steps only when needed (such as 'at any time between steps 3 and 5...'), because the timing is usually obvious and need not be stated.

To have the system act on a secondary actor only when the primary actor signals, use the idiom 'User has the system fetch the data from system B', which shows the user controls the timing and the ball passes user to system to system B without specifying the interface mechanism.

Express repetition in plain prose — either inside one step ('user selects one or more products') or as an unnumbered note after the steps ('customer repeats steps 3–4 until done') — rather than using a programming-style loop construct.

A use-case step corresponds to Jacobson's 'transaction' with four parts — the primary actor sends a request and data, the system validates the data, the system changes its internal state, and the system replies to the actor — and how many of these four parts you fold into a single step or sentence is a permitted point of writer variation.

Among valid ways to split a transaction into steps, prefer one that separates the validation and the internal state changes from the response sent back to the primary actor, but in a review or as a coach defer to the writer's preference among the valid styles.

Step numbers exist only so a step can be referenced (chiefly from the Extensions section), not because steps occur strictly in that order — the sequence is a partial ordering — so reader notes between steps need not be numbered, and whether to number at all is a low-stakes personal or project preference.

Reserve the numbered 'fully dressed' template for large or critical projects, where it enhances consistency and simplifies checking writing quality, and use the unnumbered 'casual' paragraph template — which carries the same information — on smaller projects or when the cost of locating every failure condition is not justified.

Several step-sentence organizations are equally valid — a full prose sentence, a play style of 'Actor: goal phrase', and an abbreviated-actor variant — and data passed in a step may be written as an inline comma list (good for early drafts) or broken into a tabbed list (better as precision or length grows).
Avoid two step anti-patterns: a step missing its actor (so it is unclear who acts) and a step that does not show the actor's real goal (such as 'the customer checks whether they have enough money').

Cockburn's recommended format is one column of plain prose, numbered steps, no 'if' statements, and an extension-numbering scheme combining digits and letters (2a, 2a1, 2a2); when teams are shown the same use case in competing styles they almost always choose this one-column numbered-step version.

A fully dressed use case template carries these fields: use-case number and name (the goal as a short active verb phrase), Context of use, Scope, Level, Primary Actor, Stakeholders and Interests, Precondition, Success End Condition, Failed End Protection, Trigger, Main Success Scenario, Extensions, I/O Variations, and optional Related Information.

Wirfs-Brock's two-column 'conversation' form (primary-actor actions on the left, system actions on the right) is clear but makes use cases long, does not support secondary actors, and is best reserved for a later analysis stage that details system responsibilities or the user-interface design, after the functional requirements are written.

Do not write 'if...then...else' statements in use-case scenarios: a single 'if' is harmless, but real use cases accumulate many nested 'if's that make the required behavior hard to understand, and writers who try it consistently return to the extension style.

Prefer plain natural-language prose over a formal use-case language, because prose expresses parallel, optional, asynchronous, and exceptional sequencing easily, and things that are hard or complicated in programming languages are easy to write and read in prose.

Avoid diagrammatic notations (sequence, collaboration, activity diagrams, Petri nets, CASE-tool forms) for functional requirements, because end users and executives are untrained to read them — cutting off your core readers — and tools hide the step text behind pop-ups so the use case cannot be scanned; in bake-offs readers chose plain word-processor text over diagram tools.

The UML use case diagram (ellipses, arrows, stick figures) shows only the packaging and decomposition of use cases, not their content, and cannot show step sequencing or which actor acts; never replace use-case text with ellipses, because the use case lives in its text and any diagram is only an illustration to help the reader find the text.

The only consistently useful use-case diagram is the topmost-level one showing the external actors and the user-goal use cases (equivalent to the old context diagram and the Actor-Goal list); the value of decomposing the ellipses below that level drops rapidly.

All the use-case writing forms except the use case diagram express the same basic information and the book's guidelines apply to all, so do not fuss about which format your project mandates; Cockburn prefers single-column, numbered, plain-text, full-sentence form because readers near-universally pick it, but if your readers or team lead prefer another, choose it and get on with writing.

Treat the extension conditions as where the most interesting requirements and design live: capture them in requirements, consider them in design, test for them, and work in two stages — first brainstorm every possibility, then evaluate, eliminate, and merge.
Capture all alternative conditions — both failures and alternative success paths — in the Extensions / Alternate Courses section, each patched onto the single designated main success scenario.

Finish brainstorming the failure conditions before considering how the system reacts to any of them, because failure handling consumes the energy and flow needed to build a good conditions list, whereas completing the list lets the team take a break with the use case's structure in place.

When brainstorming how a scenario could fail, deliberately consider: the primary actor sending bad data or requests, failed validation checks, non-response or failure from secondary actors, primary-actor inaction (timeouts), bad data discovered internally such as on disk, and critical performance failures of the system that you must detect.

Include internal failures such as discovering missing or bad database data in the failure list, because how the system reacts on detecting bad internal data is part of its external requirements; omitting it (each team hoping another handles it) leads to production failures like a system replying only 'No Data Found'.

Expect the brainstormed failure list to be longer than you will ultimately use and still incomplete, since you will discover new failure conditions while writing failure handling or adding validations; do your best now and plan to return and add to it later.

Reduce the extensions list with explicit criteria: include only failures you can detect; exclude mere incorrect system performance you cannot detect; add an explicit success validation only for the rare critical internal failure (for example, the ATM verifies cash actually dispensed before debiting); include internal failures whose effect reaches the outside world; include bad behavior of external actors; consider timeouts; and include any condition that requires the system to protect a stakeholder interest while excluding conditions that need no system reaction.
When in doubt whether to keep a failure condition, include it, because the damage from an extra condition is small compared with the damage of a forgotten extension.

Write each extension condition as a phrase saying what is wrong or different compared with the main success scenario (occasionally a past-tense sentence), and when steps are numbered, label the condition with the step or steps where it can occur.

Use small numbering conventions for extensions: a letter (a, b, c) after the step number for multiple conditions on one step, a colon after the condition to mark where it ends, a step range such as '2-5a' or an asterisk '*a' (listed first) for an any-time condition; these conventions make the extensions markedly easier to read.
Do not fuss over whether a failure occurs on the data-entry step or the following validation step; simply attach it to the validation step when one exists for the condition.

For each extension condition write a scenario fragment that picks up at the named step and continues in exactly the same style as the main scenario (goal level, verb style, full sentences), either reaching the goal by an alternative path or patching or abandoning the failure.

A scenario fragment typically ends one of three ways — the failed step is patched so the story proceeds as if it never failed, the blocking condition is cleared so the step restarts, or the use case aborts in total failure; in the first two cases you need not state what happens next, but in an abort the steps must still set the stakeholders' interests into place.

Most extensions need not say 'go to step xxx' because the return point is obvious and such notes reduce clarity; add an explicit 'go to step xxx' only on the rare occasion the story jumps to a non-obvious part of the main scenario.

Indent the numbering of a scenario fragment beneath its condition (2a1, 2a2), and handle a failure within a failure by continuing that indentation and condition-naming until the numbering grows too complex, at which point break the handling out into its own use case.

Delay breaking a scenario fragment into its own use case for as long as possible, because a new use case has real cost — it is cognitively more complex and must be labeled, tracked, scheduled, and maintained — so keep the fragment inline until readability suffers, roughly at three pages of text or four levels of indentation.
condition: break out a sub-use case when the inline handling exceeds about three pages or four levels of indentation

statement: Treat moving a step out into its own use case, or folding a small use case back into steps, as a small decision with no glamour or insult, because every step is already written as a goal and every use case is titled with one.

Rely on failure roll-up to avoid a scenario explosion: low-level failures roll up into a single high-level failure condition in the calling use case, which usually does not care why the sub-use case failed, only whether it exited in success or failure (the 'striped trousers' image of a goal with a success leg and a failure leg).

Use the Technology/Deferred Variations section to mark, at the highest level possible, that a step's intent is the same but a few key technologies for doing it differ (for example pay by check, EFT, or credit; or identify by card, eye scan, or fingerprint), keeping the main scenario phrase generic and rolling the variations up just as you roll up failure conditions.

The Technology/Deferred Variations section is only for marking lower-level technology variations to be handled later; putting condition or action steps there is using it incorrectly, and often the single marker fully specifies the behavior because the difference is only data format and interface technology.

In the textual goal-based style every goal phrase is a potential reference to another use case — any step can be broken out into a use case and any use case included in another — which is one of the attractions of goal-based use cases.
Whenever a step calls out a sub-use case, the writer must handle the possible failure of that sub-goal, because any sub-use case can fail.

Reserve standalone 'extension use cases' (with their own trigger naming the base use case's step and condition) for the rarest, most exceptional occasions and keep them to a minimum, never as the normal writing style, because they specifically reference the internal parts of the base use case and the base use case contains no reference back to them.

The most natural use of an extension use case is when many asynchronous services the user might request do not disturb the main flow (as in a word processor where typing is the main activity but the user may zoom, change font, or spell-check); keeping the base use case ignorant of these lets other teams add any number of extension use cases without forcing the base team to update theirs.

You are done writing all the use cases when you have identified every primary actor and all of their blue (user-goal) goals and have written all the blue use cases plus the strategic and subfunction use cases needed to support them.

All the use cases together form an ever-unfolding story — a few key primary actors with high-level goals, one strategic use case each at the outermost scope naming the user goals, unfolding into subfunction use cases — so an executive can read the top levels and stop anywhere while implementers start at the user-goal level and read down.

Everything about writing use cases applies equally to business use cases and to system use cases, and use cases describe a business process well in easy-to-read form; teams that model business processes with a different technique such as workflow or activity diagrams miss the synergy between business-process and system use cases.

A business use case describes how the organization, treated initially as a single black box, responds to a triggering event to satisfy an external actor's goal and the stakeholders' interests — exactly the Actors and Goals plus Stakeholders and Interests models applied to the company.

Because a business use case looks exactly like a system use case, the ever-unfolding story can start in business use cases and continue into system use cases, but writers and readers easily cross levels — putting system behavior into business use cases or business operations into system use cases — which loses executive readers.

To reduce confusion between business and system use cases, always mark both the scope and the level in the template, read them both, and train readers to read both at the start of every reading; because marking the fields alone is insufficient, a stronger visual difference such as a logo or typeface is desirable.

The design of the business does not directly imply the system specification: deriving the system spec straight from the business model leaves you with the same business process, whereas an improved process is invented from the core business process plus ideas about how technology can help.

Recipe for business-to-system modeling: document the stakeholders and interests, treat the whole organization as a black box reacting to external primary actors and triggering events, write black-box business use cases, then open the box and write white-box business use cases showing the internal players' essential goals, usually without naming technology.

In most business processes the computer system is not an active player but a repository or conduit between players (like a telephone), so deciding how to improve that conduit to improve the overall process is a separate act of invention and design that the use cases themselves do not answer.

Naming technology in business use cases, like naming user-interface design in system use cases, is brittle over the long timescale a business process operates; Cockburn prefers to write the business process without technology, leaving the invention open, and then to write contextual business-process steps into the system requirements use case to show how the system fits the ongoing operation.

A business use case that includes system operation is actually a specification (or documentation) of the system to be designed and is therefore redundant with the system-specification use case; how to handle that overlap is a matter of personal preference.

White-box use cases expose the system's internals and show how its parts collaborate to deliver services; the two common occasions for writing them are describing or reengineering business processes and documenting a system's design.

Attach each use case's secondary information — priority, expected frequency, performance demand, delivery date, secondary actors, open issues, completion state — at the end of the use case, and maintain a spreadsheet keyed by use-case name so the data can be resorted by actor, priority, completeness, or complexity for alternate overviews.

Use cases act as a hub that links to other information: the use case names the need for I/O data formats and complex business rules and hyperlinks out to their descriptions, making use cases the center of the requirements document even for many non-functional requirements.

Do not force requirements that do not fit the use-case (interaction) form into use cases — an algorithmic requirement such as a two-tape merge is best described with algebraic or tabular forms; roughly 25% of the requirements file suits use-case form, a central connecting portion, while the other 75% uses other forms.

Keep data descriptions out of the use case but in the requirements file, and manage their precision in three levels: information nicknames (first level), field lists (second level), and field details and checks (third level).

In the use-case text refer to data only by information nicknames (such as 'name, address, and phone number'), because writing the fields out slows requirements gathering, lengthens the use case, and makes it brittle; break the details out and link to them, since many use cases reference the same nicknames.

The second level of data precision lists the fields under each nickname; keep it separate from the use case and expect it to change as the team learns, and treat nicknamed items that appear together in a step as a signal of a useful field cluster for the user-interface designer.

Expand field details and checks (types, lengths, validation rules) — what programmers and database designers need — somewhere in the requirements file such as a data-requirements or field-definitions section, never inside the use case; the use case should link to that expansion, which changes independently over time.

When you face many near-identical use cases (Find a Customer, Find a Product, and so on) under the fully dressed template, write one parameterized use case that captures the common search-and-select logic once and uses nicknames for the parts that vary (the searchable qualities, the display fields, the sort fields), linking out to per-thing data descriptions; this keeps the use case clean, localizes the common logic, and guarantees consistency.

Put your energy into writing easy-to-read prose use cases, after which the relations between use cases (includes, extends, generalizes) become straightforward and natural; writers of text-based use cases simply do not hit the scenario-explosion and 'extends' problems that people who fiddle with stick figures, ellipses, and UML relations do.

A base use case 'includes' another when it names it in an action step; this is the normal higher-to-lower relationship and is simply the familiar subroutine call, so use it as the default way to link use cases, remembering the purpose is to communicate with a person, not a CASE tool or compiler.

An extending use case names an internal step and condition in a base use case, takes over the behavior, and returns the actor to the interrupted point — a 'patch' on the base use case — which is exactly what an ordinary scenario extension does once it outgrows its embedding use case.

Treat UML 1.3 'extension points' as a mistake: naming the extension location in the base use case violates document management because that location moves when the base is edited, and you must modify the base use case whenever a new extension point is needed — defeating the original purpose of not touching the base.

Do not use extension use cases unless you have a really good reason, and if you do, absolutely do not expose the extension points in the use case diagram, because that publishes the use case's internal parts and obscures the far more important goal name.

A use case or actor 'generalizes' another when one is a generic 'some kind of' version of the other; the pass/fail test for actor generalization is that the specialized actor can perform every use case the general actor can.

In plain prose you simply list the kinds of operations a user can do (for example 'Customer does a transaction, one of: ...') without invoking the 'generalizes' relation, whereas UML forces a modeling choice — so prefer the prose.

Avoid the generalizes relation's hazards: you cannot safely combine specialization of actors with specialization of use cases (the rule is that a specialized use case must be substitutable wherever a general one is mentioned), a mistake even use-case experts have published; if you must use it, make the generalized use case empty.

If you do draw use-case diagrams, place higher-level goals higher on the page so 'includes' arrows point down and the others up, point generalization arrows up into the bottom-center of the general use case, give each relation a visually distinct arrowhead (a triangle for generalizes), and show no use cases below user-goal level on the main context drawing.

The use case does not describe the user-interface design: a UI designer reads the use cases and invents a presentation that preserves the steps while minimizing user effort, then has it reviewed by users and programmers.

It is beneficial to paste a snapshot of the nominated GUI design at the bottom of a use case and to provide a finite-state-machine-style diagram of the screen flow, so readers can see how the screens link, without those artifacts becoming part of the use-case text.

Use-case writers can usefully pretend to fill out a screen or paper form to discover what information must be entered and any sequencing constraints, and may share these sketches with the UI designer — provided they are read as how usage experts view the task, not as requirements.

Use 'calling use case' and 'sub-use case' to mean a higher-level use case invoking a lower-level goal through the includes/subroutine-call relationship, because those terms are obvious to beginning writers and novice readers.

Because scenario-step text does not stand on its own as a line-item feature (copying it forces rewording and context, causing double maintenance), prefer on projects up to about 50 people to derive the development task list informally from the use cases — breaking out line items with a highlighter into the schedule — rather than maintaining two official documents, one usage-centered and one feature-centered.
condition: practical on projects up to roughly 50 people that stress personal communication

statement: When an organization requires feature- or line-item allocation, break the requirements into pieces each assignable to a single developer or team — programmers implement a mechanism such as Undo or a search-screen framework that is one line buried in or repeated across use cases — and make each piece a feature or design task that is estimated, assigned, tracked, and checked off.

Use the use cases as ready-made design scenarios, especially with Responsibility-Based (CRC) design which walks through scenarios; even with other techniques they remind designers when the design is complete and handles all the exceptions.

Accept that the design task does not map tidily onto use cases — a class or component is used by several use cases and key information may sit in a use case scheduled for a later release — so design each release as well as practical and expect new information to surface and force change rather than requiring designers to pre-scan every use case.

Do not force a use case to map to a release: write each use case for maximum readability and release portions of it at a time (highlighting the released parts), rather than splitting use cases per release, which is possible via extension use cases but makes the set hard to read; this assumes incremental delivery in increments of about four months or shorter.

Treat the use cases as a ready-made functional test suite available at requirements time: the test team breaks them into numbered tests with specific data values, writes at least one test case per extension (the main-success-scenario test first), and derives the performance and load tests from them, using the stakeholders and their interests to identify test cases.

CRUD operations (create, update, delete an entity) are in principle three separate use cases because each is a distinct goal possibly done by a different actor at a different security level, but writing a single 'Manage X' use case with create and delete as extensions reduces clutter; neither is wrong, so default to 'Manage X' for less clutter and split it out only when writing complexity demands.

Let project 'forces' — business and social setting, level of understanding, stakeholder needs, experience versus formality, coverage, consistency, complexity, conflict, completeness, and resources — guide how much formality, how much breadth versus precision, and how to stage the writing, while the core answer to writing consistently readable use cases stays constant given the actor-goal, full active-sentence approach.

Expect no use-case tool to be better than barely usable, and judge tools by three capabilities: scannable, sortable views across the whole use-case list, propagation of template changes to existing use cases, and automated forward and backward hyperlinks.

Prefer a word processor with hyperlinks (file per use case) over a CASE tool for use cases, because CASE tools hide the step text behind dialog boxes and are so unusable that team members revert to word processing.

To get more of the system into view at once, use four scale mechanisms: lower the precision (view only use-case names), select use cases for relevance (only the actors, team, or release under discussion), bundle use cases into clusters or subject areas, and layer them so higher-level use cases roll up lower-level ones.

Manage related use cases as a cluster (a set handled together, often collected by a strategic white use case) and, on larger projects, partition the whole into subject areas such as Invoicing or Promotions, typically with one development team per subject area.

Under incremental release, ship the highlighted parts of a use case per release rather than splitting use cases per release, because most teams prefer accepting 'release 2 delivers the highlighted parts of use case 15' over multiplying the number of use cases in the database.

Use the use-case list as the planning and tracking structure and to show each release's business value: build a table of use case, primary actor, business priority/value (from sponsors), estimated complexity (from developers), development priority, target release, and owning team; Kent Beck's Planning Game has developers estimate cost first so sponsors can set priority in light of that cost.

Follow the 12-step recipe for writing use cases: find the system boundaries (context diagram, in/out list); brainstorm the primary actors; brainstorm their goals; write the outermost strategic use cases; revise them; pick a goal to expand (optionally writing a system-in-use story); fill in stakeholders, interests, preconditions, success-end and failure-protection conditions and double-check the goals against them; write the main success scenario and double-check it against the interests; brainstorm the failure conditions; write the recovery for each; break out any sub-use case that needs its own space; then revise top-down for completeness, readability, and failures.

Run a within-use-case pass/fail checklist where every answer should be yes: the title is an active-verb goal the system can deliver; scope and level are filled in; the scope is treated as a black box (unless it is a white-box business use case); the steps match the stated level; the primary actor's goal is a service promise of the system; preconditions are mandatory, system-ensurable, and never checked inside; the success end condition satisfies all stakeholder interests; the main success scenario runs trigger to success with about 2–11 steps; and each step is a forward-moving succeeding goal with a clear actor, clear intent, clear information passed, and a 'validate' rather than 'check'.

Build readability habits: keep use cases short, build a top-down story from a strategic use case, name use cases as short verb-goal phrases, run each from trigger to goal delivery plus bookkeeping, write full active-verb sentences of completing sub-goals, keep the actor visible in every step, make failure conditions and their recovery stand out (clear what happens next without naming step numbers), put alternatives in extensions rather than 'if' statements, and use 'includes' relationships whenever possible.

Check quality across the whole use-case set with three questions: does the user-goal list capture every service all primary actors want, do the use cases form a story unfolding from the highest goal to the lowest, and is there a context-setting highest-level use case at the outermost scope for each primary actor?

Calibrate your rigor to the cost of mistakes: good internal communication between usage experts and developers lowers the cost of use-case quality failures (people simply talk and straighten matters out), while distributed, multi-contractor, very large, or life-critical projects raise it — so do not fuss over small mistakes on small casual projects but be rigorous when the consequences of misunderstanding are great.

The two mistakes you can make with a use case are writing too little and writing too much; prefer to write too little, because a short readable document actually gets read and prompts the questions that reveal what information is missing, whereas a hundred detailed low-level use cases close communication since no one reads them.

Diminishing returns set in very quickly with use cases: naming the goals and drafting the storyline is tremendously valuable, after which the energy to polish rises fast while the value flattens — so when in doubt, write less text, at a higher goal level, with less precision, in plain story form.

A bad use case is still a good use case, because merely writing use cases at all improves communication among users, executives, and developers; on small and even medium projects with good internal communication, just the main success scenario with a few failures marked in plain paragraph form can suffice, as on a 50-person project and the Chrysler C3 Extreme Programming team's single-card 'stories'.

Work breadth-first and from low to high precision rather than depth-first — primary actors, then goals, then the main success scenario, then the failure/extension conditions, then the recovery steps — rationalizing and reviewing priorities at each stage before the next, because each level costs far more effort than the previous, so trimming early saves great energy later.

Writing the recovery steps is the hardest part of use-case writing and frequently uncovers new use cases, new actors, and new failure conditions, because it forces the writer to confront business-policy matters that otherwise stay unmentioned.

Use exactly one sentence style for action steps: present tense, active verb in the active voice, describing an actor successfully achieving a goal that moves the process forward; this single style serves every kind of use case under either template, and mastering it yields use cases that are short, clear, and easy to read.

Write extension conditions in a different grammatical form from action steps so the two are not confused — simple descriptive phrases or sentences, preferably (though not always) in the past tense (for example 'Bad password', 'File not found', 'User exited in the middle') — while the action steps inside the extension again read 'actor successfully achieves goal'.

Reread each sentence to confirm the goal is in sight and is really the actor's goal: replace a non-goal such as 'system checks credit limit' with the real goal 'make sure the customer has adequate credit', and record the failure path ('insufficient credit:') in an extension.

Make the use case satisfy all the stakeholders, not just the primary actor: because use cases are the functional requirements, they must show how every stakeholder's interests are met; there are usually 3–5 stakeholders (the primary actor wanting something, the company wanting not to give value away, a regulator wanting a demonstrable log, and someone wanting mid-transaction recovery), and their interests largely repeat across use cases.

Verify stakeholder interests by writing the Success End Condition and then the Failure Protection against each stakeholder, which surfaces missing main-scenario steps (such as writing an intermediate state for catastrophic-failure logging) and missing validations; the check costs little time and is highly revealing — one team found that all of their first year's change requests were already present in the stakeholders' interests list.

Anchor the goal-level decision — the single hardest thing about use cases — on two reference points: the user-goal ('blue') level, which is what the primary actor wants from the system now before moving on to something else, and a length of roughly 3–10 steps per use case.

Because most drafted use cases sit below the user-goal level (at indigo/subfunction level), raise an under-level use case by asking 'What does the primary actor really want?' or 'Why is this actor doing this step?', taking the answer to 'why' as the real goal.

Use the empirical length signal: most well-written use cases have 3–8 steps and none longer than about 11 that could not be shortened and improved by shortening, so when a draft runs 10–20 steps check for the two beginner mistakes — including user-interface details that do not belong, and writing steps at too low a level.
condition: applies to a single use case's main scenario length

statement: Distinguish a business use case (scope is the organization's operations, an outside actor achieving a goal against the organization, usually user-goal or strategic and often white-box and technology-free) from a system use case (scope is the computer system, almost always black-box, level of greatest interest the user goal): the system use case describes the outside of the computer system while the business use case describes the inside of the business.

Always mark the scope field, and when several systems co-exist (for example a new system A piecewise replacing an old system B) write a separate blue use case for each direction with each system alternately the primary actor, using embedded graphics such as shading the system under discussion and circling the primary actor to keep the scopes clear.

When several job titles share a goal you may name the primary actor 'either A or B', say one acts in the other's role, or invent a new role (such as 'Orderer') that both fill — none is wrong, so pick what communicates to your audience and settle a single convention for the team to use consistently.

Job titles matter at a project's beginning (to brainstorm and cluster goals and to characterize user skills for the UI design) and at its end (to assign permissions, build training by skill set, and package deployment), but become insignificant placeholders in the middle as role names genericize.

Treat every use case as having two exits, success and failure, and attend to both: write and later double-check how all stakeholder interests are satisfied at success and protected under each kind of failure; a sub-use case's success exit returns to the calling step and its failure exit returns to the calling condition where that failure is handled.

Detect precondition writing errors with two checks: if an extension names the failure of a condition that the precondition asserts, or if the use case can technically start without the precondition satisfied, then either the precondition or the extension is wrong.

Do not overstate preconditions: a condition that is not actually a requirement or cannot be enforced (for example requiring that 'Evaluate order' contain at least one order item) is an overstated precondition, and the cost of such an error scales with project criticality and the strength of internal communication.

When writing a use case, write the stakeholders and their interests first, then the success end condition, then the main success scenario; and write the failure protection before the main success scenario, so the protections are built in the first time rather than discovered later and retrofitted.

Always use the 'includes' relation as the default link between use cases — the calling use case simply names the sub-use case, which is what every step already does — and reserve 'extends' and 'generalizes' for rare exceptions, since writers who follow this report they avoid the use-case confusion others describe.

Treat readability as the core value of a use case: its ultimate purpose is to be read, so you may trade away some precision and accuracy for readability, but only so much before the use case stops serving its purpose.

Recognize that the first draft of a use case captures roughly two-thirds of its value, and that while correcting and extending the conditions keeps adding value, rewording the sentences stops improving communication after a short while — so redirect that energy to the rest of the requirements (external interfaces, business rules, and so on).

When use cases serve as a functional specification, always treat the system under discussion as a black box, because teams that wrote requirements by guessing the system's internals found those use cases hard to read, poorly received, and brittle as their understanding of the internals changed.

Keep the alternative courses after the main success scenario (Jacobson's original form), because putting the branching cases inside the main body of text makes the story too hard to read and evaluate.

There is strong consensus not to describe the user interface in use cases, and writing the specification so the interface is not specified along with the function is a small, learnable, and worthwhile art.

Accept many equally valid variants within the core values — numbered steps or paragraphs, casual or fully dressed template, full sentences or theatre style, business modeling with or without use cases, use-case diagram or actor-goal list — and do not treat any single one as mandatory, choosing per project and team.

Regard a domain class or component as only ever 'complete with respect to the delivered use cases', never absolutely done, because a new path or new use case can change it; in object-oriented work adding an attribute is a minor operation, so express completeness against a named function set rather than as an absolute percentage, and expect a culture clash with the database-design mindset that wants every attribute identified up front.

Remember that use cases are fundamentally a text form and that the use-case diagram intentionally lacks step sequencing, data, and the receiving actor, so it cannot replace the text; use the ellipses only to augment the text — as a table of contents, a context diagram of actors pursuing overlapping goals, or a big picture relating higher- and lower-level use cases.

One legitimate use of the exploded use-case diagram is showing project progress by coloring each ellipse to reflect its status (for example, written and accepted, design started, delivered), giving an at-a-glance view of what is being worked on and what remains.

Remove user-interface design from a use case by rewriting it into simple one-column story form and focusing on the user's intent at each point — imagining a completely different UI that achieves the same effect proves the writing captured intent rather than interface; this preserves all the real requirements, leaves the design less constrained, and can shrink an 8-page draft to roughly a quarter of its length.

Shorten and raise the level of a use case with three moves: merge separate data-item steps under one nickname (such as name, address, and phone number into 'personal information', which also lets the data details change without touching the use case); combine pieces of information going in the same direction into one step unless they are so different that separating reads better; and replace a run of low-level steps with the single higher-level goal they serve (for example, replace open-connection / request-stock / return-stock / validate-quantity with 'system validates with the warehouse that sufficient quantity is in stock').

Avoid the missing-actor anti-pattern: a use case that lists only what the system does ('collects card and PIN, validates funds, dispenses money') without the actor's behavior is harder to understand, verify, and correct and often omits critical sequencing carried by the actor, so write full actor-action sentences that name who acts in each step.

Learn a use-case quality gradient — design scope, goal level, or step size — with Kent Beck's Three Bears pattern: deliberately overdo one extreme (far too much detail) and then the other (far too little), which makes it much easier to place a third attempt at a comfortable middle.

Recognize that an element's actor classification is relative to the chosen design scope: the same thing can be the system under design at one scope and a subsystem at a wider scope, while an owner is usually a stakeholder rather than an actor and a data carrier like an ATM card is a data item unless it has behavior of its own.

Adding a stakeholders-and-interests check while writing costs little time or energy but gives a tighter framework for thinking about what you are producing and helps you notice when you have accidentally omitted a step.

Expect a business use case's main success scenario to look trivial, because it shows how things go in the main success situation; the interesting content appears in the failure conditions and in how the organization uses the use case to nominate improvements to its IT support.

A high-level 'system' use case that seems too vague to be useful can still pay for itself three ways: it glues together the user-goal use cases within the business guidelines (showing when events like closing, purging, and archiving happen), it records sequencing and business rules unknown to part of the team (saving hours of guessing), and it serves as an introduction and table of contents for new readers and executives.

Favor prose written for a human audience because it handles complexity other forms cannot — such as a clerk who may enter data in any order while the system works asynchronously yet a normal sequence is still shown — and stop revising at an adequate version once you pass the point of diminishing returns, even after several full rewrites.

Tame sets of twisty, nearly-identical use cases with a parameterization convention: let any sentence such as 'Find a Customer' or 'Find a Product' mean 'use the use case Find a Thing with thing = X', logging the per-thing data and search restrictions on a separate linked sheet, so the common search logic is written once and reused across many similar-but-different contexts.

A high-level business use case can stay under two pages and serve as an introduction and lead-in to the user-goal use cases, and when a sponsoring executive instantly spots an omission as out-of-scope it confirms the writing was pitched at the right level.

An approximate, informal use case can be sufficient for the job — a good use of diminishing returns — as when a three-programmer co-located team never took their use cases beyond a rough draft yet still captured the logistics in the extensions and variations and the data they were obliged to record, using acronyms and a cut-down template.

Treat a use case as a 'marker intended to remind': it takes real effort to write because the writer must double-check the exact procedures, extensions, variations, and required data, but once written it reminds the team of what they once knew, which justifies acronyms and a cut-down template for a small co-located team.

Write a loop inside an extension by flattening the repetition into named conditions rather than deep nesting: for an ATM that allows three PIN tries before keeping the card, the most readable form separates '1st and 2nd incorrect submission: reprompt' from '3rd incorrect submission: keep card, log, notify', avoiding a deeply nested recursive version.

Account for the roughly 100-to-1 difference in effort between writing a readable use case and reading one: an 18-page, drawing-heavy service description was replaced, after a week of intense work, by a much shorter use-case description that made the problem appear simple.

Use white-box use cases to document the internal design of a framework or system — describing how its components collaborate, such as a Resource Lock's behavior — and capture each point of policy variability as a separate 'apply X policy' sub-use case.

Write use cases through an effective sequence: start as a group (brainstorm the primary actors and their goals, review the actor-goal list, and write one system-in-use story together so everyone gets the feel), then break into pairs to draft, circulate the drafts for peer comment, review with a designer and a usage expert, hold a full group review, and only then baseline the use case.

Draft use cases in pairs, because two people raise many questions about the business rules, distinguish real requirements from old-days holdovers, and cross-check that the user interface has not crept in and that the goals sit at the right levels.

Gather review comments on paper and make one merged editing pass rather than editing online suggestion-by-suggestion (which causes thrashing as a change made for one reviewer is reverted for another); include a designer to confirm there is enough detail to implement from (excluding data and UI design) and a usage expert to confirm the requirements are true, and after a full group review baseline the use case and change it only when mistakes are found.

Use cases free users to focus on the what (their intentions and how the system is used) rather than the how (the physical screens), so keep use-case discussions separate from screen-layout discussions to minimize disagreement over trivial issues and let participants focus on what matters in their expertise.

Expect use cases to surface different or changed requirements: validating previously frozen requirements (such as an RFP) against current needs with the client often changes the original scope of the project, so plan for re-scoping.

You cannot elicit the right use cases without the right people in the room — the real operators, analysts, investigators, and their supervisors — and it is better to have too many people and viewpoints than too few; when you cannot predict which users are needed, stage a kick-off with representatives from every user area to schedule the right sessions.

Do not spend more than half of each workday in elicitation sessions, because processing the raw material gained in a session takes as long as eliciting it, and the other half day is needed for housekeeping, planning, and preparation.
Use a fast, accurate scribe who stays a silent partner — not joining the session interaction or editorializing except to clarify what is being captured.
Expect to miss some secondary actors (such as a supervisor) in the initial actor list, especially roles not represented in the room, and watch for missing use cases that reveal them.

Break elicitation writer's block by first having users write, at a high level, the steps of their daily activities and then locating where the system is used, because that daily-work context frees them to think of uses of the system — one team went from blocked to twenty use cases the next day.

Do not expect use cases 'by the pound': elicitation is a creative activity with peaks and valleys, rushing it is counterproductive, and when people get stuck use catalysts such as prompting handouts and deliberately controversial viewpoints that provoke participants to express their own views.

Treat eliciting use cases as a social activity that needs social lubricants, and reduce redundant copying between use cases by defining standard descriptors and standard system-responsibilities, success, and failure scenarios so sessions can focus on the exceptions.

Help users separate role from job title with a concrete device — for example physical caps labeled with actor-role names that a person 'wears' when using the system — because users find it hard to accept that an actor role can differ from a job title.

Build, maintain, and display an assumptions list and open sessions with a reading of the assumptions to stop re-arguing settled points, and post the cumulative use cases on the walls (even out of sequence) because scanning them helps participants grow familiar and write new ones faster.

Keep the use-case template as slim as possible, and recognize that past roughly fifty use cases a word processor is no longer enough — you need automation with real textual search, easy update, and reporting.

Choose a use-case standard fit to your situation from five nominated standards — business process modeling, requirements elicitation even if use cases will not be the final form, drafting/sizing system requirements, functional requirements on a short high-pressure project, and detailed functional requirements at the start of an increment on a longer project — and tune it per the book's principles, since simply selecting among the five clarifies your group's position.

For business process modeling, make the organization itself the system under discussion, use only two scopes (the organization as a black box for the top-level and outermost use cases, and organization-operations as white-box for the internal design) and two goal levels (strategic and user-goal), deliver the final use case fully dressed, and use casual forms only for early sketching and elicitation.

For drafting and sizing system requirements, use the casual template — accepting that it omits information — to sketch the requirements fast enough to estimate the size and shape of the system, then later either elaborate them into fully dressed use cases or design directly from the casual drafts.

For requirements elicitation when use cases may not be the final form, move quickly through casual drafts in a lively work session and retain the stakeholders and interests (to remind people of hidden requirements) while not worrying about other aspects that may be recast into another format.

Do not estimate from the use-case count alone — also account for algorithmic complexity, technology infrastructure, and development-staff capability — though as a rough yardstick one project delivered about 160 task-level use cases in roughly 20 programmer-years, about eight use cases per programmer-year, or one use case per six programmer-weeks.

Normally write scenarios in generified form, using placeholders for the primary actor's identity and the values passed, and reserve a concrete scenario — one that names every actor and actual value, like a true past-tense story — for a system-in-use story that also shows the actors' motivations and intentions as a light warm-up to use-case writing.
Use a use-case brief — a one-paragraph synopsis of the use case — as the lightest-weight form, below the casual and fully dressed templates.
Software requirements is fundamentally a communication problem between the people who want the software (to use or sell it) and the people who will build it.
Neither the business side nor the technical team should dominate the requirements conversation; when either side dominates, the project suffers.
condition: during requirements communication

statement: When the business side dominates requirements, it tends to mandate both functionality and dates without regard for whether developers can meet them or understand what is actually needed.
When developers dominate requirements, technical jargon displaces the language of the business and developers lose the chance to learn real needs by listening.
Resource allocation should be treated as a problem shared between customers and developers; projects fail when that burden falls entirely on one side.
