A software project cannot be perfectly predicted up front, because users change their opinions as they see early versions and software effort is inherently hard to estimate.
Spread decision-making across the whole duration of the project, making decisions frequently from the information at hand, rather than making one all-encompassing set of decisions at the outset.
A requirements document should be written only when it helps achieve the real goal of delivering software, never as a goal in its own right.
condition: only when it helps deliver working software

statement: Because written language is a thin, easily-misinterpreted medium for expressing software requirements, frequent conversations among developers, customers, and users should replace heavy written specifications.
A user story records just enough detail to avoid forgetting and to support estimation and planning, while still encouraging direct communication about the requirement.
A user story describes a piece of functionality that will be valuable to a user or a purchaser of the system.

A user story has three aspects—the Card (a short written description used for planning and as a reminder), the Conversation (which fleshes out the details), and the Confirmation/tests (which document details and determine when the story is complete).
The written card is the most visible part of a user story but not the most important; the substantive details live in the conversation and are captured as confirmation tests.
Story cards should represent customer requirements rather than attempt to fully document them.

Write stories so the customer can value them; technical implementation details such as programming language or connection-pool usage do not make good stories, unless the system's own user is a programmer (for example an API).
exception: unless the user of the system is itself a programmer, e.g. an API

statement: Prefer having more, smaller stories over having stories that are too large.
As a rule of thumb, size stories so that one or a pair of programmers can code and test each one in between about half a day and two weeks.
A story that is too large is called an epic, and an epic should be split into two or more smaller stories.
Do not keep splitting stories until every last detail is its own story, and do not decompose stories hierarchically the way a traditional requirements document numbers sub-requirements.
Handle a story's missing details through a conversation between the development team and the customer at the point when those details actually become important.
A few annotations on a story card are acceptable, but the conversation is the real agreement; stories are not contractual obligations, and what was agreed is documented by the story's tests.
Capture the users' expectations for a story as acceptance tests, for example written as short reminders on the back of the story card.
Acceptance-test reminders are deliberately short and incomplete and can be added or removed at any time; their goal is to convey enough about the story that developers know when they are done.

Because a single all-knowing customer is almost never available, establish a customer team of those who ensure the software meets users' needs, which may include testers, a product manager, real users, and interaction designers.
On a story-driven project, customers and users stay involved throughout the project rather than appearing only at the start and the end as in a waterfall process.
Customers and intended users should take an active role in writing the user stories, especially under Extreme Programming.

The customer team, not the developers, should write the user stories, because each story must be in the language of the business so the team can prioritize it, and because the customer team as product visionaries is best placed to describe the product's behavior.
Choose one iteration length (typically one to four weeks) collaboratively and keep that same length for the whole project.
By the end of each iteration the developers are responsible for delivering fully usable code for some subset of the application.
Velocity is the amount of work (story points) a team completes in an iteration; the first velocity estimate will be wrong, but it can still be used to sketch a rough release plan.
Build a release plan by sorting stories into per-iteration piles in priority order, where the estimates in each pile add up to no more than the team's estimated velocity.
Before each iteration the customer team can make mid-course corrections to the plan, and once iterations complete the team should plan with the actual measured velocity instead of the estimate.

A release is made up of one or more iterations; release planning balances a projected timeline against a desired set of functionality, while iteration planning selects which stories go into the current iteration.
Prioritize stories by considering desirability to a broad base of users, desirability to a small number of important users or customers, and cohesiveness with related stories.
Developers may suggest priority changes based on technical risk or complementarity, but the customer team makes the final prioritization in the way that maximizes value delivered to the organization.
Stories cannot be prioritized without considering their cost, where a story's cost is the developers' estimate expressed in story points reflecting its size and complexity relative to other stories.
Acceptance testing verifies that each story was developed to work exactly the way the customer team expected when they wrote it.
Include a dedicated, skilled tester on the customer team to handle the more technical testing tasks such as automating tests.

Write acceptance tests as early in the iteration as possible (even slightly before it), because doing so communicates the customer team's assumptions to developers earlier and can remind developers of cases they would otherwise forget.

Because stories shift emphasis toward conversation and away from documents, important decisions are captured in frequently-run automated acceptance tests rather than in documents that are unlikely to be read.
Each user story represents a discrete piece of functionality that a user would do in a single setting, which makes stories an appropriate unit for planning.
Stories support iterative development: write a large placeholder epic for a feature you want eventually, and refine it into smaller stories only when you are ready to build it.
Deferring detail is valuable because it lets you avoid investing thought in a feature until you are sure the feature is actually needed.
A good user story should satisfy six attributes captured by the INVEST acronym: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimatable, Small, and Testable.
As much as possible avoid dependencies between stories, because dependencies create prioritization and planning problems and make estimation harder.

Resolve a problematic dependency between stories by combining the dependent stories into one larger independent story or by splitting them along a different dimension; if neither works, put two estimates on the card (one if done first, a lower one if done after).

Stories are negotiable: a card is a short description whose details are worked out in conversation, so it need not contain every detail, though important details known at writing time should be added as brief annotations.

Avoid putting too much detail on a story card, because readers mistake extra detail for extra precision and completeness, stop talking to the customer, and specifying detail too soon often just creates rework.
Details that have already been decided through conversation should be recorded as tests (the back of the card), leaving the front of the card holding the story plus notes about open questions.
Distinguish a user (someone who uses the software) from a purchaser (someone who buys it); a valuable story need not be valued by users, since some legitimate stories are valued only by purchasers.

Avoid stories that are valued only by developers (for example, 'all connections to the database go through a connection pool'); rewrite such technical needs in terms of their value to users or customers so the customer can prioritize them.
Keep both user-interface assumptions and technology assumptions out of stories.
The best way to ensure each story is valuable to the customer or users is to have the customer write the stories.
Developers must be able to estimate (or at least guess) a story's size or the time to turn it into working code.
A story is commonly not estimatable for one of three reasons: the developers lack domain knowledge, the developers lack technical knowledge, or the story is too big.
When developers lack the domain knowledge to estimate a story, they should discuss it with the customer who wrote it to gain a general (not exhaustive) understanding.

When developers lack the technical knowledge to estimate a story, run a spike—a brief, timeboxed experiment to learn just enough to estimate—turning the unestimatable story into a spike story plus the real work story.
When a story is too big to estimate, disaggregate it into smaller constituent stories.
It is sometimes useful to write an epic as a placeholder for a big part of the system you are consciously deferring, assigning it a large, rough estimate.
Story size matters because stories that are too large or too small cannot be used in planning; the right size depends on the team, its capabilities, and the technologies in use.
Epics fall into two kinds: a compound story (several shorter stories bundled together) and a complex story (one that is inherently large and hard to break apart).
Split a compound story into constituent stories, but do not over-split into stories that are too small; group them (for example by create/edit/delete) or split along the boundaries of the data.
When a complex story is large because of uncertainty, split it into an investigative (spike) story and a separate development story, and always put a timebox around the spike.

When possible, schedule the investigative spike story in one iteration and the dependent stories in later iterations, because only the spike can be estimated and combining them raises the iteration's uncertainty.

Breaking the unestimatable research out as its own story lets the customer prioritize the investigation separately from the new functionality, avoiding the false assumption that the feature will ship in the estimated timeframe.
Combine stories that are too small (such as bug reports and minor UI changes) into a single larger story of roughly half a day to several days, then name, schedule, and work it like any other story.
Stories must be written to be testable, because passing its tests is what proves a story is done; an untestable story leaves developers unable to know when they are finished.

Untestable stories commonly arise from nonfunctional requirements; rewrite vague nonfunctional stories into measurable, testable form (for example, 'new screens appear within two seconds in 95% of cases' instead of 'the user never waits long').
Automate tests wherever possible—aim for roughly 99% automation rather than 10%—so that regressions in incrementally-developed code are caught as early as possible.
A small subset of tests (such as usability tests) cannot realistically be automated and may require a human-factors expert observing representative users; such stories are still testable.
exception: except for tests like usability that require human observation

statement: Avoid absolute words like 'never' or 'always' in stories; instead of proving something never happens, target and measure that it rarely happens against a defined threshold.
To the extent possible, write stories to be independent so they can be developed in any order.

Writing all stories from the perspective of a single user type is a fallacy that causes the team to miss stories for users outside the primary mold, so identify user roles and personas before writing stories.
A user role is a collection of defining attributes that characterizes a population of users and their intended interactions with the system; aggregate individual users into such roles.
Use four steps to model user roles: brainstorm an initial set of roles, organize the set, consolidate the roles, and refine the roles.

Brainstorm user roles with the customer and as many developers as possible by writing role names on cards with no discussion or evaluation, continuing until ideas stall (rarely more than about fifteen minutes).
Each user role should represent a single individual user rather than an organization, because a company as a whole cannot use the software.
Organize the brainstormed role cards spatially so that the amount of overlap between cards reflects how much the roles overlap.
Prefer user roles that represent people rather than other systems; add a non-human or system role only when doing so gives a direct, tangible benefit to thinking about the system.
exception: unless a non-human/system role gives a tangible modeling benefit

statement: Consolidate equivalent or heavily-overlapping roles and discard role cards for roles unimportant to the system's success, focusing on the roles that can make or break the project.

Refine roles by giving each useful attributes; standard attributes worth considering are frequency of use, domain expertise, general computer/software proficiency, proficiency with the software being built, and the user's general goal for using it.

Treat advanced role techniques (personas, extreme characters) as optional; most teams should stop after basic role modeling and use the extra techniques only when a direct, tangible project benefit is anticipated.
A persona is a concrete, imaginary representation of a user role, given a name, a face (photo), and enough relevant detail that the whole team feels they know the person.

Create personas only for one or two primary or vital user roles rather than for every role, and ensure enough market and demographic research has been done that the personas truly represent the target audience.
condition: only for one or two primary/vital user roles

statement: Stories become more expressive when written in terms of a specific user role or persona instead of the generic 'the user', and doing so does not prevent other roles from performing the story.
Considering extreme characters (users with exaggerated personalities) can surface stories that would otherwise be missed; it is a low-investment, optional technique.
Do some user-role modeling even when you have real on-site users, because having real users does not guarantee you have the right users or the right mix of them.

Reject the 'elicit/capture' framing of requirements—requirements are not pre-existing things fully known by users—and instead adopt the 'trawling' view: requirements come in different sizes, mature and change over time, and skill matters in finding them.
Even though you cannot write every story up front, still make an initial pass writing the stories you can, accepting that many will be at a high level of detail.
Look ahead roughly one release (about three to six months) and write stories whose level of detail decreases as the time horizon increases, rather than detailing far-future stories.
condition: for stories within about one release / three to six months

statement: Because stories evolve continuously, use story-gathering techniques that are lightweight and non-obtrusive enough to apply more or less continuously.
The main techniques for gathering stories are user interviews, questionnaires, observation, and story-writing workshops, and a business analyst (when available) should do much of this trawling.

Interview real users across different user roles whenever possible; simply asking 'what do you need?' is insufficient because users are poor at expressing their true needs, and having the problem does not make a user qualified to design the solution.

Use open-ended, context-free questions to surface a user's real needs, avoiding closed-ended questions and questions that imply an answer or preference; start context-free and only later move to specific questions.

Questionnaires are useful for gathering information or prioritization from a large user base about stories you already have, but they are inappropriate as a primary means of trawling for new stories because they allow no follow-up, are one-way, and have a time lag.
Observing real users work with the software reveals insights and real needs that are obscured by the users' own descriptions, which is one reason to release software early and often.

A story-writing workshop—developers, users, and the customer writing as many stories as possible without yet prioritizing them—is the most effective way to quickly trawl for stories; hold at least one before each planned release.

Run a story-writing workshop by combining brainstorming with low-fidelity (paper/whiteboard) prototyping that maps high-level conceptual workflows rather than actual screens and fields, working through each user role or persona.
Walk a low-fidelity prototype depth-first (follow one path to its end before backtracking) rather than breadth-first, which is disorienting.
Throw away or erase the low-fidelity prototype within a few days of creating it, because it is not a long-term development artifact and keeping it causes confusion.

While walking a prototype, prompt for missing stories with questions like what the user would do next, what mistakes they could make, what could confuse them, and what extra information they might need, and keep a parking lot of issues to revisit.

During a story-writing workshop focus on quantity over quality, write on cards, and do not judge or debate ideas, so that quieter participants contribute and the discussion stays high-level rather than designing screens.
Achieve the best story-gathering results by using a combination of methods rather than overrelying on any single one.
Include one or more real users on the customer team, because only a real user truly knows how they want the software to behave; resort to user proxies only when enough real users cannot be obtained.
Choosing the right user proxies is critical, so weigh each proxy's background and motives, since (for example) a marketing-background proxy approaches stories differently than a domain expert.

Treat the users' manager as a poor proxy unless she is also a true user, and even then expect her usage patterns to differ; managers can be sources of inflated misinformation, so corroborate their claims with real users.
exception: unless the manager is also a genuine user of the software

statement: A development manager is one of the worst proxy choices (unless the software targets development managers), because of conflicting goals such as favouring new technology or a bonus tied to a completion date, and a lack of hands-on user or domain experience.
exception: unless the software being built is targeted at development managers

statement: A salesperson over-weights the story whose absence lost the last sale and lacks a comprehensive product view, but salespeople are excellent conduits to real users and should be used that way.

Domain experts are ideal for building the domain model and identifying business rules, but workflow and usage stories are better obtained from actual users, and a domain-expert proxy risks producing software usable only by similar experts.
Marketing groups understand markets rather than users and tend to favour the quantity of features over their quality; they are useful for high-level priorities but weak on specific story details.
A former user is an acceptable proxy only when her experience is recent and her goals and incentives are aligned with those of real users.
condition: only when the experience is recent and incentives align

statement: Distinguish customers (those who make the buying decision) from users; weigh customers' desires because they pay for the software, but remember a customer is not necessarily a user.
Trainers and technical-support staff as proxies bias the product toward trainability or supportability rather than what real users would prioritize.

Business or systems analysts can be good proxies when they balance technology and domain knowledge and actually talk to users; beware analysts who intuit needs without researching them or who over-invest in upfront activities.
When access to real users is blocked, establish a user task force of real users to act as a sounding board while the proxy remains the final decision-maker.
When no real user is available, use more than one proxy of differing types (for example a domain expert plus a marketer) to avoid building for a single person's needs.

When working without real users, study competing commercial products as a source of stories and release the product early (even as a beta) to expose mismatches between the proxy's thinking and real users.
Do not assume that developers can stand in for users; developers generally have even more shortcomings than proxies for representing real users.

Build the customer team by adding real users first, naming a single project champion to provide one consistent customer voice, identifying the project's critical success factors, and supplementing with proxies whose strengths balance others' weaknesses.
Use acceptance tests, rather than lengthy 'the system shall' requirement statements, to capture the details that emerge from conversations between customers and developers.

Treat testing as a two-step process: jot test notes on the back of story cards whenever someone thinks of one, then later turn those notes into full tests that demonstrate the story is correctly and fully coded.

Acceptance tests capture the customer's assumptions (such as how to handle missing data) and provide the criteria for deciding when a story is fully implemented, helping avoid putting in too much or too little effort.
Write a story's acceptance tests before programming begins on it, because seeing the tests reminds programmers of cases (such as a declined card) they would otherwise forget.
The customer must specify the acceptance tests because the software fulfils the customer's vision, though developers or testers may augment them with additional tests.

Treat testing as part of the development process rather than something that happens after coding; specifying tests is often shared by a product manager (organizational goals) and a tester (a suspicious mindset), continuing as story details are worked out.

Discover additional tests by asking what else the programmers need to know, what you are assuming about the implementation, whether there are circumstances where the story behaves differently, and what can go wrong.
Keep writing acceptance tests only while they add value or clarify the story; do not write redundant tests for cases already covered by an equivalent test.

The customer is not responsible for every possible test because a good programming team unit-tests the low-level cases; the customer should focus on tests that clarify the story's intent to developers.

Because acceptance tests show the application is acceptable to the customer, the customer should execute them, running them at least at the end of each iteration and re-running all prior iterations' tests since later work can break earlier code.
Automate acceptance tests where possible, because the cost of running all prior iterations' tests grows with every iteration.
Tools such as FIT and FitNesse let customers write acceptance tests in a familiar table or spreadsheet format, greatly reducing the effort to identify and write tests.
Beyond functional story testing, the customer and team should jointly decide which additional testing types apply, such as user-interface, usability, performance, and stress testing.
On an agile project, test to find and eliminate bugs rather than to chase 100% code coverage or every boundary condition, using intuition, knowledge, and experience to focus the test effort.
On an agile project treat testing as collaborative rather than antagonistic—no 'gotcha' or blame when a bug is found—and let whoever is best equipped do the testing.
To identify stories, start by considering each user role and the goals that role has for interacting with the software, then generate stories from those goals.

When splitting a large story, write replacement stories that each deliver end-to-end functionality through all architectural layers ('slice the cake') rather than splitting along horizontal technical layers, which yields stories that are useless on their own.

Prefer full end-to-end story slices because exercising every architectural layer reduces the risk of discovering last-minute problems in a layer and allows releasing partial functionality that still works all the way through the system.

Write closed stories—ones that finish with a meaningful goal and give the user a sense of accomplishment—by rewriting open-ended ongoing activities (like 'manage ads') into discrete completed actions.
Balance the desire for closed stories against the competing need for stories small enough to estimate and schedule into one iteration, yet large enough to defer capturing details until necessary.

Annotate a requirement that must be obeyed rather than directly implemented as a 'Constraint' card; such cards are not estimated or scheduled but serve as reminders, and where possible an automated test should verify the constraint is not violated.
Size stories to their implementation horizon: write near-term stories small enough to plan into upcoming iterations, and write more distant stories larger and less precise.

Keep the user interface out of stories as long as possible to avoid mixing the requirement with a solution; UI detail will inevitably enter later as stories shift from new functionality to modifications of existing functionality.
exception: UI detail legitimately enters once stories modify or extend existing functionality

statement: User stories are not appropriate for every requirement; when some aspect (such as UI guidelines or a system-to-system interface) is better expressed in another format, use that format.
exception: for requirements like UI guidelines or external system interfaces, use another format

statement: Include the user role when writing a story (for example 'A Job Seeker can post her resume' rather than 'A user can…') to keep real, tangible users in the developer's mind.
The role-based story template 'As a (role) I want (function) so that (business value)' helps capture the role and value and can help distinguish important stories from frivolous ones.
Write each story for a single user, because doing so surfaces ambiguities (such as whether a user can remove only her own resume or also others') that a plural phrasing hides.
Write stories in the active voice (for example 'A Job Seeker can post a resume' rather than 'A resume can be posted by a Job Seeker') for readability.

Responsibility for writing the stories resides with the customer and cannot be passed to developers, because the customer must understand each story to prioritize it and writing them is the best way to gain that understanding (developers may assist).
Do not number story cards, because numbering adds pointless overhead and pushes discussion toward abstract numbers instead of tangible features; use a short descriptive title as shorthand instead.
Remember that a story card's main purpose is to remind people to have a conversation; keep cards brief and do not let added detail replace the conversation.

A good story-estimation approach lets you revise estimates as you learn, works for both epics and small stories, is quick, shows progress and remaining work, tolerates imprecision, and supports release planning.
Estimate stories in story points—a team-defined relative unit (an ideal day, an ideal week, or a measure of complexity)—rather than in precise calendar time.

Prefer treating a story point as an ideal day of work, because estimating in ideal time is easier than estimating elapsed time and gives a better foundation for later converting estimates into calendar time.
Own story estimates collectively at the team level rather than by an individual, because the eventual assignee is not yet known and team-derived estimates are more useful.
Involve as many developers as practical in estimating; the customer answers questions during estimation but is not allowed to give her own estimates or editorialize about the developers' estimates.
Estimate with an iterative, Wideband-Delphi-style process: gather the customer and participating developers, read each story aloud, let developers ask questions, and converge on an estimate.
When estimating a story, include every activity needed to complete it—coding, testing, talking with the customer, helping plan or automate acceptance tests—not just the coding.

Have each developer write a private estimate and reveal all estimates at once; treat divergent estimates as useful and have the high and low estimators explain their thinking (without it feeling like an attack) to surface hidden assumptions.
Re-estimate after a brief discussion and repeat while estimates keep converging (rarely more than three rounds), aiming for a reasonable shared estimate rather than absolute precision.

Triangulate estimates by comparing a story to already-estimated stories (a four-point story should be about twice a two-point story) to keep the meaning of a story point stable over time, for example by pinning cards on a wall by size.
Velocity is the number of story points a team completes in an iteration, and one iteration's measured velocity is the best forecast of future iterations of the same length.

Use measured velocity to predict future velocity provided nothing unusual affected this iteration's productivity, the estimates were generated consistently, and the iteration's stories were independent.
condition: provided productivity was normal, estimates were consistent, and stories were independent

statement: Because summing many independent estimates is approximately normally distributed, biased per-story estimates still let a team use one iteration's velocity to predict future iterations, though the prediction is weaker with few very large stories or when the team is still learning.
Whether or not a team pair-programs has no effect on story-point estimates; it only changes the velocity number, not the actual speed of work.

Constrain estimates to a predefined non-linear scale (such as 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 20, 40, 80) because estimation precision legitimately decreases as story size increases, so arguing over seven versus eight points is false precision.

Story points are relative to a single team and are not comparable across teams, and when a story or epic is split into smaller stories or tasks the sub-estimates need not sum to the parent's estimate.

Developers should define story points in a way usable by their team, stick to that definition consistently, give honest estimates without yielding to pressure for low ones, estimate as a team, and keep estimates consistent across comparable stories.
Most software projects do best with a new release every two to six months, and even projects that can release more frequently benefit from grouping related features into a release.
Begin release planning from a product roadmap of themes (the main focus areas for the next few releases), expecting and welcoming the roadmap to change as you learn more about the product and market.

Plan a release toward a range of acceptable dates rather than a single fixed date, because an iterative process makes the date easy to fix but the scope hard to fix, and a date range gives more timing flexibility.
exception: unless the date is genuinely fixed, e.g. for a trade show or key-customer milestone

statement: Prioritize stories with the MoSCoW scheme (Must have, Should have, Could have, Won't have this time) to avoid tedious arguments over high/medium/low categories.

Sort stories using both technical factors (risk that the story cannot be completed as desired, and the impact on other stories if it is deferred) and customer factors (broad desirability, importance to a few key users, and cohesiveness with related stories).

When developers and the customer disagree on the implementation sequence, the customer decides every time, but the customer must use the developers' estimates and prioritizes to maximize the value delivered to the organization.
Share each story's estimate with the customer because cost changes priority: a story the customer ranked high when she thought it was cheap will often drop once she learns it is expensive.
If a customer struggles to prioritize a story, split it so that its more- and less-essential parts can be prioritized separately.

Agile prioritization favours doing the highest-value 'juicy bits' first rather than the riskiest parts first, which enables early release and defers possibly-unneeded infrastructure—while still considering risk, with the customer (informed by the technical team) deciding whether to pull risky stories forward.

Developers are responsible for flagging stories that can be safely deferred but will become much more costly to add later (such as infrastructural or scalability needs), without using that as license to push their favourite technical features into early iterations.

Make an implicit infrastructural or nonfunctional need visible to the customer by writing a user-facing story that forces it (for example a deployment story that requires the middle tier), so it can be prioritized.

Select an iteration length jointly (typically one to four weeks); shorter iterations give more frequent course correction and visibility at a small per-iteration overhead, so err toward slightly too short.
Keep the iteration length constant for the project so it falls into a steady rhythm, changing it only deliberately for a known reason rather than randomly.
Convert total estimated story points into a project duration using velocity (for example, 100 ideal days at a velocity of 25 implies about four iterations).

Obtain an initial velocity by, in order of preference, using historical values from the same team on a similar project, running one initial iteration, or—when neither is possible—taking a reasoned guess.

When guessing initial velocity with a story point defined as one ideal day, expect velocity to be roughly one-third to one-half of the developer-days available in an iteration because of interruptions, and refine the estimate after the first few iterations.
condition: when a story point is defined as one ideal day of work

statement: Build the release plan by allocating the highest-priority stories into each iteration up to the planned velocity, filling successive iterations until all stories are placed.
Do not put too much faith in the release plan: it yields an approximate duration (for example 'about 5-7 iterations'), not a precise calendar date.

Use the release plan to set initial expectations and then continually reset them, monitoring each iteration's velocity and re-estimating stories whenever you learn something that changes the estimates.
Prioritize stories into a precise sequence (first, second, third) rather than into coarse buckets like high/medium/low.
The customer should give honest release deadlines and avoid padding the date (do not say June 15 when the real need is July 15).
Build the release plan on realistic estimates that include an appropriately sized project buffer, and resist inflating the priority of infrastructural or architectural work.
At the start of each iteration, plan one level deeper than the release plan, since release planning leaves only a coarse allocation of stories to iterations.
Hold an iteration planning meeting attended by the whole team—the customer and all developers including testers—so the customer can answer detailed questions about the stories.

Run iteration planning in the sequence: discuss a story, disaggregate it into constituent tasks, have one developer accept responsibility for each task, and finally have each developer estimate their accepted tasks to check they are not over-committed.

In iteration planning, have the customer read each story in priority order and let developers ask only enough questions to disaggregate it into tasks, deferring fine details to after the meeting to keep it efficient.

The customer should resist changing story priorities mid-iteration, because frequent changes whipsaw the team; an adequate working solution is usually worth keeping over a hypothetically better one that must be built from scratch.

Disaggregate stories into tasks because a story may be shared across developers and because converting a story into tasks (a short burst of just-in-time design) surfaces work that might otherwise be forgotten.
Remember that stories describe user- or customer-valued functionality and are not developer to-do lists, whereas tasks are the developer-facing units of work.

When disaggregating, separate a task that is hard to estimate from the rest of its story, split tasks that different developers could do in parallel, and break out a part whose independent completion is valuable.

Give each task a single responsible owner (even when pair programming), while the whole team shares responsibility for completing all tasks and keeps responsibilities fluid, so no one ends an iteration saying their own work is done while a teammate's is not.

After covering the customer's top velocity-worth of stories, have each developer estimate their tasks in ideal time and confirm the total is realistic; if over-committed, the options are to keep and hope, hand tasks to a teammate, or ask the customer to drop or split a story.
Velocity is the number of story points completed in an iteration, and the team should review it both at the end of and during each iteration.

Count only fully completed stories toward velocity, at full value, and exclude partially completed stories, because partial completion is hard to quantify, implies false precision, delivers no user value, and hides the complexity lurking in the last 10 percent.

Recurrent partially-completed stories signal that stories are too large or that the team lacks teamwork; respond by writing smaller stories and by swarming to fully finish some stories rather than partially completing all of them.

Calculate velocity from the story-point estimates assigned before the iteration and never retroactively change a completed story's points (a four-point story counts four even if it should have been seven), while still using the lesson to adjust future estimates.
Generally plan the next iteration's velocity to be no more than the previous iteration's, planning higher only when the team is genuinely convinced a story was estimated too low.
exception: unless the team is truly convinced a prior story was underestimated

statement: Avoid over-reacting to a single iteration's velocity, because an initial velocity is volatile; wait two or three iterations for a longer-term view and track planned-versus-actual velocity and cumulative story points together.

An iteration burndown chart shows the story points remaining and reflects both completed work and added or re-estimated scope, so it does not reveal the team's raw speed and must be read alongside a velocity or cumulative-story-point chart.

Agile teams start without a complete upfront specification because customers cannot know everything in advance, so expect stories to be added, dropped, resized, and re-prioritized as everyone learns more.

During an iteration, maintain a daily burndown chart of the estimated hours of work remaining, gathering each team member's remaining-effort estimates (for example on a shared whiteboard) and totalling them about once a day.

Keep each task's hours-remaining estimate current to reflect the owner's latest thinking about work left (whether or not work has started), updating whenever a task finishes or at the end of the day, and let people raise an estimate as comfortably as they lower it.
Track hours remaining rather than hours expended, because what matters is the effort left, and tracking time spent feels like micromanagement and adds imprecise overhead.

Add a new task mid-iteration only when a forgotten task is needed to complete a story already in the iteration; genuinely new desired work must be prioritized into a future iteration at the next planning session.
exception: unless the new task is a forgotten one needed to finish a story already in the iteration

statement: Make progress charts big and visible, posting them in a common area so the whole team and stakeholders can see them.
Chart defects per story point to detect whether increases in velocity are coming at the expense of quality.
Complete one story before moving on to the next, preferring a few fully completed stories over a larger number of partially completed ones.
IEEE 830-style 'the system shall' requirements specifications are tedious, error-prone, and time-consuming, and become so long that no one reads them fully, obscuring the big picture.

A warning sign of a failing specification-driven project is two groups repeatedly rewriting essentially the same requirements document under different names, positioning themselves for end-of-project blame; shifting to conversations removes this because nothing feels contractually final.
It is effectively impossible to write all of a system's requirements up front, because users change their minds once they see the software being built.

Reject the 'change of scope' framing for evolving requirements, because it falsely assumes scope was ever fully definable and wrongly treats software as complete when it satisfies a requirements checklist rather than the users' goals.

Requirements lists push attention onto a checklist of system behaviours rather than the user's goals, and reading a list nudges designers toward premature solutions; framing needs as the user's goals yields a better solution.

With an IEEE 830 specification the cost of each requirement is invisible until the whole document is written, wasting effort on requirements that will not be built; attaching an estimate to each story up front lets the customer see cost as she selects work (a customer must see the price of each wish-list item).

Because a requirements list describes the software's behaviour rather than the user's goals, ask 'how and why will this feature be used?'; turning a feature list into usage scenarios often reveals features that are not actually needed.

A use case is a generalized description of interactions between the system and its actors; each path through it is a scenario, with a Main Success Scenario as the primary path and Extensions as alternate or error paths.

A user story is smaller in scope than a use case because its size is constrained for scheduling; a story is roughly equivalent to a single scenario, and a story plus its acceptance tests approximates a whole use case (story to main success scenario, tests to extensions).
Use cases are typically permanent artifacts maintained for the life of the product, whereas user stories are not meant to outlive the iteration in which they are implemented and are often discarded.

Use cases are more prone than stories to embedding user-interface and implementation assumptions; prefer essential use cases stripped of technology assumptions, whose user intentions map directly onto user stories.

Use cases and stories serve different purposes: a use case documents an agreement readable by customer and developers and results from analysis, whereas a story facilitates release and iteration planning and is a placeholder that initiates analysis conversations.

An interaction-design scenario is a detailed description of a user's interaction with the system and is typically larger than even a use case, so a single scenario may span multiple use cases and many user stories.
User stories differ from interaction-design scenarios mainly in scope and detail: scenarios carry far more detail and usually cover the work of several stories.

Writing requirements down shifts the team's focus to a shared document and away from shared understanding, so customers receive the developers' interpretation of the written words rather than what they actually wanted.

Written words are imprecise and can carry multiple meanings, whereas a conversation removes ambiguity through a short feedback loop and mutual learning, without the false appearance of precision or a signed-off record to point back to.
The goal of a user story is not to document every detail of a feature but to record a few short placeholder sentences that remind developers and customers to hold future conversations.

Pursuing 'perfect requirements' is the wrong goal, because users refine their opinions as they learn and perfect individual requirements do not sum to a perfect whole; aim instead for adequate stories augmented with frequent conversations.

User stories are comprehensible to both business people and developers because they are terse and always written to show customer or user value, unlike jargon-heavy IEEE 830 documents and even more so than use cases or scenarios.
People remember events better when those events are organized as stories, including recall of both stated and inferred actions, which favours the story format for requirements.

User stories are the right size for planning—small enough that planning, programming, and testing can proceed without further aggregation or disaggregation—whereas IEEE 830 statements are too fine-grained and nested to prioritize separately and use cases or scenarios are too large.
If two requirement items cannot be prioritized or developed separately, do not write them as separate items; if they are split only so each can be tested, write the tests directly instead.
User stories suit iterative development because you can write some stories, code and test them, and repeat, splitting an epic into smaller stories progressively as detail is needed.

An IEEE 830 document implies that anything not stated as 'the system shall' is excluded, making it impossible to tell a missing requirement from an unwritten one, whereas stories support progressive levels of detail.
User stories avoid the 'completism' trap of template-driven use cases, because there is no standard set of fields that people feel compelled to fill in for every story.
Stories encourage deferring detail by letting you write a placeholder goal-level story and add detail only when it becomes important, which makes them well suited to time-constrained projects.

Software cannot be built strictly top-down from a complete set of requirements, because users do not fully know what they want, many details emerge only during development, humans cannot comprehend that many details, changes occur, and people make mistakes.

Developers actually work opportunistically, shifting freely between requirements, usage scenarios, and design at varying abstraction levels, and user stories support this because they are easily written and rewritten at any level of detail and embrace change.

User stories encourage participatory design, in which jargon-free stories engage users as active participants in designing their software, rather than empirical design where designers study users who never truly participate.
Face-to-face conversation around stories accumulates tacit knowledge across the team, growing as developers and customers talk more often.

On a large project with many stories it is hard to see the relationships between stories; mitigate this by using user roles and keeping stories at a moderate-to-high level until the team is ready to develop them.
condition: on large projects with many stories

statement: When a process mandates requirements traceability, augment stories with lightweight supplementary documentation (for example a per-iteration document linking stories to their test names) rather than abandoning stories.
condition: when requirements traceability is mandated

statement: Story-based face-to-face communication does not scale to very large teams, where some information must be written down; weigh the trade-off between many people knowing a little via documents and fewer people knowing a lot via high-bandwidth conversation.
exception: on very large teams where conversation cannot disperse information widely enough

statement: Understand why your team chose its requirements technique and know the alternatives, applying another technique (such as a use case or interaction-design scenario) when you and the customer cannot reach a shared understanding of a feature.

A frequent need to revise estimates is a smell that stories are too small, because a small story's estimate swings with implementation order and overlap; combine overlapping small stories for planning and split them only when slotting them into an iteration.

Difficulty planning iterations because of dependencies between stories is a smell caused by stories that are too small or inappropriately split; fix it by combining the interdependent stories or re-splitting them as full end-to-end slices.

Developers adding unplanned features or over-interpreting stories ('goldplating') is a smell; keep developers focused on the customer-prioritized stories, and have a developer with a new idea suggest it to the customer for a future iteration rather than building it unasked.
Prevent goldplating by increasing visibility of what each developer is working on—through brief daily meetings, end-of-iteration demos to the customer, and QA involvement.

Spending too much time gathering details well before a story is implemented, or writing about stories more than talking about them, is a smell of over-valuing documentation; use small cards (and a smaller card if you run out of room) to constrain detail.
Writing stories with user-interface detail early in a project is a smell; avoid binding stories to UI elements that may not exist yet and phrase them around the user's goal instead.
exception: UI detail is acceptable later once the interface is known

statement: Wanting story templates, finer-precision estimates, or a software tool not justified by team size is a smell of thinking too far ahead, common in teams used to big upfront requirements; remember that most requirements cannot be known in advance and good software emerges through iterations.

Occasionally splitting a story during iteration planning (because it is too large or mixes high and low priorities) is normal, but splitting stories frequently is a smell; respond by taking a pass through the remaining stories and pre-splitting those that should be split.

A customer who has serious trouble prioritizing is a smell usually caused by stories that are too large (replace them with smaller ones) or not written to express business value (rewrite so each story's value is clear, ideally by having the customer write them).

When a customer refuses to write or prioritize stories—often a symptom of a blame-avoidant culture—give her a non-threatening, sometimes private way to express opinions while you take responsibility for the final decisions.
User stories are not tied to Extreme Programming and work well as the requirements approach for other agile processes such as Scrum.

An iterative process makes progress by successive refinement of a whole, while an incremental process builds and delivers complete, fully-tested pieces; Scrum and XP are both iterative and incremental.

Scrum runs in fixed-length sprints (traditionally about thirty days); at the start of each sprint the self-organizing team pulls work it can complete from the prioritized product backlog into a sprint backlog, and inspects progress in a daily scrum.

A Scrum team (about four to seven developers) is self-organizing with collective ownership and an all-in-this-together attitude and avoids fixed role labels, supplemented by a product owner (who owns and prioritizes the backlog) and a ScrumMaster (a servant-leader who removes obstacles and upholds the rules).

The product backlog is the master prioritized list of desired functionality; rather than writing every feature up front, capture the obvious items and let the backlog grow and be reprioritized as you learn more.

Hold a sprint planning meeting at the start of each sprint where the product owner describes the highest-priority items, the team asks questions and alone decides how much to commit to, and together they define a short sprint goal.

Once a sprint begins, only the team may add work to it—not the CEO, sales, or even the product owner—and in exchange the organization commits not to change the sprint's contents; if a truly significant change is required, abort the sprint and re-plan.
exception: unless the team is ahead of schedule and asks the product owner for more, or the sprint is aborted and re-planned

statement: Each sprint must deliver a potentially shippable product increment: coded, tested, usable software the organization could choose to ship.

Hold an informal sprint review that demonstrates working software (no slideshows, minimal preparation) and assess the result against the sprint goal, where achieving the overall goal matters more than completing every individual item.

Hold a short (about fifteen minutes, often standing) daily scrum where each member answers what they did yesterday, what they will do today, and what obstacles block them, making commitments to peers rather than to a manager.

Keep the daily scrum to its three questions: note issues and resolve them afterward in a smaller group rather than designing or problem-solving in the meeting, and do not turn it into an estimates-and-numbers grilling (update estimates separately).
Use the daily scrum's shared snapshot to rebalance assignments, for example having a developer who is ahead pair with or take over tasks from one who is behind.
Prefer the least time-consuming and least-intrusive method of gathering and sharing project information.

Constrain the Scrum product backlog to user stories—each describing value to a user or the product owner—because doing so makes the backlog far easier for the product owner to prioritize and trade off than a mix of features, defects, and technical tasks.
Initially stock a Scrum product backlog by first identifying user roles and then writing the stories for each role, combining Scrum with a powerful requirements-identification technique.
Stories make sprint planning easier and faster because each backlog item delivers customer-assessable value (unlike technology-driven items) and disaggregates readily into tasks.
Composing the Scrum product backlog entirely of user stories makes the sprint review easier, because each item of customer or user value is straightforward to demonstrate.
Stories keep the daily scrum focused on customer and end-user intent and help the team judge, mid-sprint, whether a story has been developed far enough or too far.

In one reported rewrite, a seven-person Scrum-with-stories team delivered comparable functionality to a waterfall effort using far less effort (about 54 versus 540 person-months, and roughly 840 versus 120 source statements per person-month), suggesting stories plus Scrum can be far more productive than waterfall.
Not every requirement should be forced into a user story; most projects have some requirements—often nonfunctional ones—that stories cannot adequately express.
Handle nonfunctional requirements as constraints written on a card annotated 'Constraint', and where feasible write an automated test (run at least daily) to verify compliance.
exception: some constraints, like 'written in Java', cannot or need not be tested

statement: For nonfunctional requirements too complex for a constraint card, communicate them in whatever additional format is appropriate or traditional (for example a data dictionary).
Paper note cards suit stories because they are simple, encourage interaction and sorting, and their limited writing space reminds people stories are imprecise and caps the detail added.
Prefer a software story-tracking system over note cards when the team is not collocated, when stakeholders are remote, or when ISO-style requirement-to-test traceability is mandated.
condition: when the team or stakeholders are remote or traceability is mandated

statement: Neither note cards nor software is best for every situation; match the tool to the project and team, starting with cards and switching to software only when there is a compelling reason.

Iterative refinement is fine for changes beneath the user interface, but changing a user interface that users have already learned harms them, so if the UI is important to the product's success design more of it up front and treat 'change the UI as little as possible once started' as an unwritten constraint.
exception: when UI changes stay below the interface and do not affect what users have learned

statement: Apply a story-based Agile Usage-Centered Design sequence when the UI matters: user-role modeling, trawl high-level stories, prioritize, refine high- and medium-priority stories, group related stories, build a paper prototype, refine it with users, then start programming—keeping the whole effort lightweight (days to a few weeks).

When uncertain which user-interface technology to choose, writing two user interfaces hedges the decision and keeps the middle tier honest by preventing functionality from being wrongly pushed into the client tier.

Retain completed stories rather than discarding them (archive the cards or keep the software/report), because retained requirements have repeatedly proven useful for process audits, product rewrites, and contractual requests.
Treat a bug report as its own story when fixing it would take about as long as a typical story, and combine many quick-to-fix bugs into a single story for planning purposes.
Colored cards to denote story types are optional and often not worth the overhead; use them only if they genuinely help you organize, otherwise keep the process simple with plain cards.
When the real customers are external to the company, designate an internal customer who acts as a proxy to help identify and write the stories.
In a story-writing workshop, writing stories in any order and working role-by-role are both valid approaches that should yield the same set of stories.

Because development is incremental and iterative, the customer need not think of every story up front; a story thought of after work has started can be moved into the release by moving out roughly the same amount of work.
When a story's interpretation could materially change its estimate, ask the customer to clarify before estimating, and split the story when a natural, easy division appears.
The customer attends the estimation meeting only to clarify and must neither give estimates nor visibly react to them, since an audible reaction undermines the estimation effort.
Create a release plan in four steps: select an iteration length, estimate the team's velocity, prioritize the stories, and allocate stories to one or more iterations.
When facing a fixed near-term deadline, use short iterations so the team can measure its real velocity after the first iteration before committing the remaining work.

The XP customer role writes the stories, prioritizes them, and writes and executes the acceptance tests; the customer need not be a user and is often a product manager, project manager, or business analyst.
When a project has multiple customers they must speak with one voice, most commonly by designating one customer-team member as a 'first among equals'.
XP programmers share responsibilities across roles and are expected to write automated unit tests for everything they write.
An XP coach monitors the team's use of the practices and nudges them back on track, while the project manager acts more as a leader who shelters the team from bureaucracy and removes obstacles.
XP's twelve practices are synergistic and interdependent, so adopt all of them and defer dropping or customizing any practice until you are experienced with standard XP.

Under 'small releases', deliver each feature fully within a single short iteration—never half a feature and never the full feature at half quality—and treat the iteration as a firm timebox, adjusting the amount of work (not the end date and not quality) to fit.
Select an iteration length that is as short as possible while still delivering tangible business value, and when undecided between two lengths choose the shorter one.

Refactoring restructures code to improve it without changing its external behaviour; XP requires (not merely encourages) refactoring whenever you touch code that needs it, which prevents gradual code decay and substitutes for big upfront design.

In test-driven development, write the test before the code in a short test-code cycle and write operational code only in response to a failing test, which keeps code well-factored, testable, and maintainable.

Studies of pair programming found that for roughly a 15% increase in total programming time it yields lower defect counts, less code to solve the same problem, faster problem-solving, broader code understanding, and higher developer satisfaction.
Pair programming matters in XP because it sustains the discipline that other practices (such as always refactoring or always testing first) require, which is easy to skip when working alone.
Work at a sustainable pace, because a team moving at a consistent brisk pace achieves more over time than one working at a pace it cannot sustain; let the team set its own pace and watch for burnout.
Practice collective code ownership—all code owned by everyone so any pair can change any code—relying on a strong automated unit-test suite to guard against unintended side effects.
Because the team collectively owns the code, adopt a shared coding standard, keeping it as brief and essential as possible.

Pursue the simplest design that delivers the needed features, judged by Beck's four criteria: the code and tests fully convey intent, there is no duplicated code, and the system uses the fewest classes and the fewest methods.
Adopt a system metaphor as a shared, simplified frame of reference for how the team thinks about the system's behaviour.
Integrate continuously—at least daily—so that each check-in triggers a full build and automated test suite and integration problems are fixed immediately in very small batches.

Keep the customer on-site as part of the development team to write stories and acceptance tests and answer questions immediately, which is essential to the user-story approach because of the conversations it requires; a remote customer introduces delays that disrupt progress.
exception: a remote customer works only with extra tooling and at the cost of delays

statement: XP rests on four values—communication (favouring face-to-face over written documents), simplicity (solving today's problem rather than an anticipated future one), feedback (the more immediate the better), and courage (for example to refactor, backed by automated tests).
A team is doing XP if it lives by XP's five principles—rapid feedback, assume simplicity, incremental change, embrace change, and do quality work—even if it omits one or two of the twelve practices.
Use-Case 2.0 adapts ideas from user stories and agile or lean methods into a lightweight use-case-driven development practice.
Use-Case 2.0 applies use cases beyond requirements to architecture, design, testing, user experience, business modeling, and software reuse.
Use cases should drive development by structuring the team's selected practices without prescribing a specific management, design, implementation, or testing method.
Use-case slices make use cases workable as backlog and flow items while linking requirements work to architecture, design, testing, planning, business modeling, and reuse.
Use cases provide more operational value than standalone user stories by scaling detail and connecting development concerns.
condition: For larger systems, larger teams, or complex and demanding development contexts.

statement: Adopt use cases by keeping stories simple, preserving the system view, focusing on value, slicing work, delivering increments, and adapting to the team.
Use stories to communicate required behavior, align participants on goals, and organize both successful and problem-handling paths.
Establish a whole-system view before deciding what to include, what to exclude, what the system will cost, and what benefit it will provide.
Frame requirements around the value created by actual system use rather than around long inventories of functions or features.
Structure a use-case narrative so the simplest successful path is separated from variant and problem-handling paths.
Use the flow structure of a use-case narrative to identify test cases that complete the story definitions.
Build systems with many dependent requirements as user-value slices instead of attempting to build the whole system in one pass.
exception: This guidance is aimed at systems with substantial work or requirement dependencies.

statement: A practical slicing workflow is to select valuable behavior, split it thinner, define acceptance tests, choose a central end-to-end slice, estimate as a team, and then build.
Treat a use-case slice as spanning requirements, design, implementation, test cases, and test results rather than as a requirements-only artifact.
Deliver software as a sequence of demonstrable or usable increments and releases instead of as a single undifferentiated delivery.
Vary the detail and formality of use-case narratives according to collaboration style, distribution, contractual constraints, criticality, and team needs.
condition: When team context, risk, or communication needs differ.

statement: Organize Use-Case 2.0 around three linked concepts: use cases for requirements, use-case slices for scoped work, and stories for stakeholder exploration.
Scope-manage each use case by splitting it into independently workable slices that each carry customer value.
Use stakeholder stories to bridge stakeholders, use cases, and use-case slices and to discover the slices that should drive implementation.
Define a use case around behavior that produces observable value for a particular user and groups related functional requirements.
Track use-case and use-case-slice states as waypoints for understanding, implementation, and testing progress.
Use a use-case slice as the work item and placeholder for all design, implementation, and test work needed for selected stories.
Allow different slices to be prepared, analyzed, implemented, and verified concurrently instead of interpreting slice states as a project-wide waterfall.
Describe stories through flows, special requirements, and test cases, including both functional and nonfunctional threads.
Keep each story on a coherent flow path from the start of the basic path to its completion so it remains complete, goal-related, and complementary.
Start work products at the bare-essential level and add detail only when communication problems, special circumstances, or critical requirements demand it.
Use a use-case realization to describe how system elements collaborate to perform externally described use-case behavior.
Prioritize and estimate use cases and use-case slices, then address the most important ones first.
Run Use-Case 2.0 activities iteratively and in parallel: find actors and use cases, prepare slices, analyze interactions, implement and test slices, and verify the combined system.
Define test cases for each slice before implementation so slice work can support test-driven development.
Continuously inspect and adapt use cases, slices, slice size, and work-product detail as priorities, lessons, and change requests emerge.
Apply use cases to any system that is used, including embedded systems, machine-interaction systems, and process-control systems.
condition: When the system has observable usage behavior, whether or not human interaction dominates.

statement: Use use cases recursively for business modeling by modeling business interactions and then the systems needed to support or improve the business.
condition: When analyzing business requirements or business-process change.

statement: Capture nonfunctional requirements either inside the relevant use cases or as separate infrastructure use cases for cross-cutting technical capabilities.
condition: When the requirement is tied to a use-case step, service level, or shared infrastructure concern.

statement: In backlog-driven approaches, make use-case slices the primary backlog items because their structure supports independence, value, testability, estimability, negotiation, and further slicing.
condition: When using Scrum-like or other backlog-driven iterative approaches.

statement: In one-piece flow approaches, flow use-case slices rather than whole use cases because slices can be kept small and regular enough for throughput control.
condition: When using Kanban or another one-piece-flow approach.

statement: Tune Kanban boards and work-in-progress limits to the team structure and working practices instead of treating any single board design as definitive.
condition: When visualizing use-case-slice flow with a board or explicit work-in-progress limits.

statement: Under waterfall governance, increase work-product detail to compensate for upfront handoff and reduced face-to-face story sharing.
condition: When development must operate inside waterfall-style governance or third-party handoff constraints.

statement: Use state and handoff tracking to adapt Use-Case 2.0 to existing team structures, monitor flow, and improve team performance.
condition: When work moves through people, specialist teams, or handoff points.

statement: Use-case slices and user stories share practical backlog-item traits: sprint-sized functionality, further splittability, lightweight representation, acceptance tests, conversation support, and estimability.

Use cases and use-case slices add value beyond user stories by supplying a system view, deeper behavioral understanding, better test-asset organization, impact analysis, scope management, scalable documentation, and missing-or-redundant functionality detection.
Choose between user stories and use cases based on context rather than personal preference, especially subject-matter-expert access and the severity of escaped requirements errors.
User stories are a good fit when subject-matter experts are easy to access and escaped requirements errors would have low severity.
condition: When domain experts are readily available and the cost of requirements mistakes in production is low.

statement: Use cases and use-case slices are more suitable when subject-matter-expert access is limited or requirements errors would have high consequences.
condition: When expert access is poor or escaped requirements defects are costly, unsafe, contractual, or otherwise severe.

statement: Use cases and use-case slices can scale down to the lightweight situation served by user stories and scale up when the system context grows.

Use user stories alone only when the system is expected to remain in the low-error-severity, high-expert-access context; consider use cases and slices when future growth may move it outside that context.
condition: When choosing the requirements technique for a system whose future complexity or risk may change.

statement: Use-Case 2.0 is compatible with common engineering practices such as continuous integration, intentional architecture, and test-driven development, as well as common management practices.
Use-Case 2.0 can support agile or lean teams through lightness and flexibility while also supporting formal or waterfall environments through completeness and rigor.
